value.detail: Section 2.1 prints h(x)=sum h_k(x), then sums V(h_k,a_k,t), with directions a_k not bound in that displayed expansion and the node t suppressed in the norm notation. The source calls these functionals norms. Constant functions have zero variation, so they are seminorms unless an additional quotient or normalization is intended. The text defines |A| as cardinality, but writes a partition P={z_0,...,z_|P|}, containing |P|+1 points. The sum and indexing are preserved rather than silently renumbered.

The projection interval uses min/max even though tree cells can be relatively open or unbounded. The printed smallest-minimizer explanation says T_opt precedes every pruned subtree, without limiting the comparison to minimizing subtrees. The optimization definition and this wording are retained; the natural minimizing-subtrees interpretation is not substituted into the original.

The statement that collapsing a node decreases unpenalized empirical squared error conflicts with least-squares node means. This is not used as a replacement for the explicit penalized optimization defining T_opt.

Assumption 4 quantifies over every K>=1 with a fixed finite A at a given n. Under the printed finite-sample stopping rule, a nonempty sample always leaves a terminal node with at least one observation, whereas An/2^K tends to zero. Thus the literal unlimited-depth quantifier needs clarification if the same stopped tree family is used for arbitrarily large K. The source is not silently restricted to feasible depths.

Node means require nonempty children, but the displayed optimization permits all real b and all candidate directions. Candidate nonemptiness, tie selection, and empty-child handling are not explicitly specified. The source finite-values argument establishes attainment only once the criterion and admissible splits are defined.

A tree stopped at its root has no ordinary internal nodes. Section 2.3 adds a formal empty node for the orthogonal expansion, but does not specify a search set or split-success probability for it, nor explicitly state whether that augmentation applies to the oracle maximum. Thus either a maximum-over-empty convention or a formal-node probability convention needs clarification. Zero success probability also requires an extended-real reciprocal, possibly multiplied by zero variation. The separate non-vacuous integrability discussion does not impose Assumption 1 on Theorems 1 or 5.

Section 2.2 declares d to be a positive integer bounding the number of nonzero coordinates. It does not explicitly add d<=p, although choosing an effective bound no larger than p is natural. The logarithmic terms and tiny sample sizes also need boundary conventions (n=1 or N=1 can make complexity terms zero). These parameter restrictions are not invented.

The positive-constant statement for gamma is followed by the separate gamma=infinity convention for bounded responses. The meaning of B^infinity at boundary thresholds is not stated; the natural 4/gamma=0 interpretation of risk exponents is recorded separately.

The text states without-replacement subsampling and independent copies of Theta, with all trees sharing the original sample. Independence is therefore read conditionally on that sample. Its original formula is archived; the census uses the earlier geometric projector definition without silently correcting the display.

An arbitrary empirical subset Gram matrix can be singular even when the full design has row rank n. The main text neither specifies generalized inverses nor a coefficient selection convention for extending a fitted n-vector to a population function in such cases. The geometric empirical projector is still unique; its full coefficient representation need not be.

The covariance coefficient vector is identified with the coefficients of a conditional expectation. For a general subgaussian design that expectation need not be linear. The original covariance condition and population L2 projection are retained, and the extra interpretation is not imposed as a new theorem hypothesis.

OMP selects by correlation divided by the original column norm. For fully refitted candidate models, the decrease in squared residual is instead proportional to squared residual correlation divided by the squared residualized-column norm. The claimed equivalence with maximizing the next-step decrease need not hold for correlated columns. The displayed algorithm remains the defining procedure.

The s-sparse branch permits s=0, leaving the displayed minimum over an empty support without an explicit convention. The gamma-sparse branch permits gamma=1; empty or zero coefficient subsets then lead to a zeroth power of zero. Neither an endpoint exclusion nor a convention is inserted into the original.

A coefficient sequence may meet both sparsity alternatives. The formulas are interpreted for the chosen hypothesis branch; they are not asserted equal where both apply. The support-coverage threshold and population-bias threshold remain distinct.
The defining condition uses a strict less-than bound whereas the claimed restatement uses less-than-or-equal. The source (CovB) statement is preserved with the strict sign.
The source prints B_m^2 : a = instead of the usual assignment punctuation. The original anomaly is preserved; the preceding decomposition and following bias norm identify the intended quantity.

The source calls sigma-hat squared a noise-level estimator without explicitly giving a nonnegative range. Theorem 5.1 permits C_tau=0; a negative estimate could make the stopping set empty even after residuals vanish. Interpreting a variance estimator as nonnegative is conventional, but it is not inserted into the theorem. Infinite stopping times and argmin selections require conventions not stated here.

The source writes an argmin as a single iteration without prescribing how ties are resolved. Nonnegative integer indexing comes from Algorithm 1; the prefix optimization (5.6) prints only m<=tau. No specific tie-breaking convention is invented.

The lower bound for tau_two-step and its risk bound in Theorem 5.1 concern the corresponding common high-probability event. The latter is not converted to an expectation bound or a new independent event.

The theorem explicitly states tau_two-step >= tilde-m, not merely tau >= tilde-m. The preceding discussion on page 22 focuses on the first-stage stopping time; the theorem's stronger printed conclusion is retained without importing appendix proof content.

value.detail: The source is arXiv:2210.13008v3, stamped 27 January 2024, 34 pages. This audit does not establish textual identity with the journal typesetting.

Both numerator and denominator are p_(D,f), making the printed log ratio zero. The immediately following proof uses p_(D,f0) in the denominator. The original definition and its use in Theorem 12 remain unchanged; this unresolved source discrepancy is material to the neighborhood condition.

The symbol F first denotes a general positive C2 parameter class, is specialized to f>=1/4 for prior (17), then is explicitly reset to a general f_min class before Theorem 12. The latter does not inherit the Gaussian prior or boundary support restrictions.

Theorem 2 assigns Pi to theta; (17) assigns Pi to f=f_theta. Posterior expectations are understood in their printed coordinate. E[f_theta|data] and f_(E[theta|data]) are different objects; only the latter occurs in Theorem 2.

value.detail: Sufficient regularity and an appropriate prior are not fully quantified in Theorem 2 itself. The source explicitly points to Theorems 9 and 10; their detailed setting and the posterior-mean paragraph are archived. No claim is made for arbitrary Gaussian priors or for the optional algebraic rate absent its condition.

Theorem 4 says in the setting of Theorem 3, but its supremum prints an Hs ball and positivity without the explicit C2 norm bound of Theorem 3. Both source clauses are retained; the census does not silently change the supremum to a norm-sum ball.

The infimum includes all measurable bounded-L2-operator-valued estimators, while the loss uses an H2-to-H2 operator norm. An arbitrary bounded L2 operator need not map H2 into H2. The source does not state an extended-infinity convention or restrict the estimator class further.

Theorem 7 refers to (12) for gamma. The adjoining text gives 1/3 under an interpolation invoking s>=2 and qualitative gamma(s) approaching one with smoothness. It gives no complete explicit formula for all s>d, particularly when d=1 and s<2. The reference and qualification are preserved.

The source asserts that Euclidean distance-neighborhood enlargements of the hyperrectangle have smooth boundaries for every m. Such offsets generally have joins between flat and curved pieces and need not have a C-infinity boundary. The displayed domain and the assertion are preserved separately from the general smooth-domain requirement; no alternative smoothing construction is invented.

The general diffusion setup normalizes volume to one, whereas the geometric construction retains width w>=2 and a positive enlargement. The explicit O_(m,w) is not volume one as written. The normalization is kept as an ambient convention with this scope discrepancy, rather than changing the geometric definition or automatically adding a unit-volume hypothesis to Theorem 8.

The source calls indices 0 through K the first K eigenfunctions, although there are K+1 including the constant mode. It also prints mixed strict and non-strict signs in the eigenvalue ordering. These are preserved without imposing simplicity. The estimator basis instead uses 0 through J-1.

The defining empirical matrix has zero coefficients outside both retained index ranges. The expected full-L2 operator is therefore a two-sided compression, while the next paragraph writes only pi_EJ P_D,f. The defining estimator is preserved and the discrepancy is separately documented.

KL is defined for arguments in F, introduced as a positive C2 class. Theorem 11 instead explicitly assumes Proposition 2B, whose opening condition is C1 with Hs bounds for s>d. Those bounds alone need not yield C2 for every allowed s,d. The source does not explain whether F additionally restricts this theorem; both clauses are retained without silently upgrading its stated regularity.

Page 5 defines integer-order Sobolev/Hölder spaces explicitly but the theorems allow real s; the fractional Sobolev convention is left standard rather than given an invented formula. The same paragraph calls the HS norm a norm on operators on a Banach space; the actual theorem applications use the Hilbert space L2. Page 17 ends a squared-dual-norm comparison with an unsquared L2 norm, retained only as source prose.

The logarithmic modulus contains reciprocal operator difference. At equality of the two operators the printed expression requires a limiting endpoint interpretation, consistent with the ensuing injectivity sentence; the source does not define that endpoint separately.

The posterior-mean paragraph writes the preceding polynomial tilde-delta_N rate without restating its spectral hypothesis. Theorem 10 distinguishes the baseline logarithmic rate from an optional polynomial rate, and Theorem 2 states only consistency. The proof shorthand is not promoted to an unconditional theorem conclusion.

value.note: The source calls E(X_h tensor X_0) a covariance without subtracting means. A main-text search for zero, mean and centering, together with inspection of the definitions and assumptions, found no process mean-zero restriction. No missing centering hypothesis is inserted.
The replacement field uses the absolute index k before a supremum over t; the stationary reduction later anchors X_k with replacement at zero. This indexing difference is retained.

Earlier p>0 wording differs from the p>=1 Bochner convention. Actual S1 results retain Assumption 3.2 II and high moment requirements; the S2 relaxation in the remark is not applied. The identity branch prints p>=6, while a proof-technical p/2 integer comment is not promoted to an extra theorem hypothesis.

The printed estimator divides by floor(eta N), has a single interpolation factor on the final self-product, is zero for floor zero, and has an unclosed parenthesis. Its claimed path continuity and positivity do not follow from these formulas and window conditions without further qualifications. No conventional replacement estimator or positive-definite window restriction is substituted.

The display uses k_f, whereas the following line defines kappa_f. The two kappa regimes share their boundary and both stated bounds are retained there. N=T^alpha is printed without integer rounding; the growth exponent alpha differs from the later significance level.

Upsilon starts as an operator on continuous S_r paths, but its time derivatives are given in L(S1) and the displayed map is evaluated pointwise. The original typing is retained without inventing a stronger operator field.

The source switches L1 to L in the D_r formula. Square roots are not holomorphic at zero; the finite-rank recommendation alone does not specify subspace identification, treatment of zero extension, or the eta=0 endpoint. Appendix E is not read.

Point evaluations at U_M are specified on an L1 space, which normally consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes. A representative or sufficient time regularity must be supplied; the source formula is preserved.

Gamma and Sigma are defined only by (B.11) and (B.12). Those formulas and joint covariance details remain unresolved because appendix bodies are excluded. Corollary 3.1 uses tau without squares where Theorem 3.1 uses tau squared.

The main-text consistency condition is saved as A4. The exact choice of p as a function of rho and kappa is deferred to Theorem C.3 and remains unresolved; the heuristic p=7 is not a universal replacement.
Formal composition and explicit expansions disagree about extra h and eta inside phi. A7 preserves both expansions, including unclosed outer parentheses; D16/D20 preserve the formal definitions.
The author uses the word linear for a specified scaling identity, with a path-valued right-hand side lacking an explicit eta evaluation. Additivity is not substituted.

The second factors are conjugated, while the quadratic form uses ordinary transpose despite permitting proper complex Brownian motions. V_k and U have squared-entry notation, not matrix squares. Limiting nonsingularity does not supply a finite-sample inverse convention. The extra closing parenthesis in (3.37) is retained.
The theorem writes a positive diagonal function on all I using positive-entry matrix notation, whereas (3.34) allows nonnegative g and the examples vanish at eta=0. The source difference is retained.

The dotted sequence counts multiplicities; the undotted sequence lists distinct values. The ratio of eigenvalue sums equals the trace version only with the appropriate multiplicity interpretation. The specialized theorems retain their simple-spectrum conditions.

The complex Hilbert-space rearrangement is printed without conjugate-space qualifications. The separability ratio also prints integration limits with differentials in the opposite order from the later theorem. Neither is silently rewritten.

The source equates a spectral density with moments of cumulative Z, maximizes a complex inner product without an explicit real-part or modulus convention, and identifies cross-spectrum singular-vector maximizers with marginal leading eigenfunctions. Those identifications require additional justification and are preserved as source assertions. The ratio is not replaced by a different standard canonical-correlation definition.

Theorems 3.3-3.5 allow sigma=0; Theorem 3.6 omits a separate sigma qualifier. Following claims about pivotal statistics still require the positive-definite limit and nonsingularity conditions of Theorem 3.2. The Gaussian-limit statements do not acquire those additional assumptions.
The marginal eigenvalue chain contains a comma before its last eigenvalue rather than another greater-than sign. The statement is retained exactly.
The first argument of population r_d lacks eta, although the next display defines an eta-dependent mean square root. Both are retained without substituting a normalized stationarity measure.
T_d denotes a deviation r_d in Section 2.4 and an accuracy s_d in Section 4.2. This source-local change is recorded; the two are related by s_d=1-r_d in the nested-model setup.

Equation (4.4) prints f_d(eta) B_d eta) - g_dd(1) B_d(1), with a missing opening argument parenthesis and a different f/g placement from (4.1). The original formula is retained rather than repaired to the expected pivotal expression.

Equation (2.18) uses strict > with Latin v and a following prose subscript/superscript typo. The later equality case s_d*=nu conflicts with that definition. The hypotheses (4.9) and (2.17), however, are equivalent under the strict definition and monotonicity; there is no separate error in that equivalence.

The first-exceedance estimator uses lower q_alpha, while the accuracy rejection rule uses upper q_(1-alpha,d0). The limiting variables may depend on d and need not be independent. No finite search cutoff, empty-minimum convention or quantile continuity restriction is specified.
Consistency is asserted for any alpha_T tending to zero, without a rate restriction. This is recorded as the source claim, without adding uniform-tail assumptions or certifying its proof.

value.note: The abstract describes lfdr as the probability that a null hypothesis is false. Equation (2) explicitly defines it as P(H_i=0 | p_i=t), meaning the null is true. The actual definition is preserved; the abstract wording is not used to reverse the event.

The density-ratio formula is a version of a conditional probability given a continuously distributed p-value. Pointwise values at zero-density points are not specified; the endpoint pi_0=0 can produce 0/0 away from the support. The max-lfdr definition assigns zero to an empty set, and the empty-rejection term in (11) must likewise be read as zero without evaluating an undefined H_(0).

Non-increasing f_1 gives the required non-decreasing lfdr in the nondegenerate mixture setting. The converse need not identify the shape of f_1 when pi_0 is 0 or 1. The source equivalence is preserved, and Theorems 5/6 explicitly restrict pi_0 to (0,1).

The last-minimizer rule and p_(0)=0 are explicit. Theorem 1 prints ell<=1 without an explicit lower bound; Theorem 4 does not print an ell range. Ell is used as a nonnegative testing level in context. The constrained rule uses p_(k)<=lambda despite the prose below lambda. The k>=0 range implicitly ends at m because only m order statistics exist. No change is made to either original statement.

Equation (7) uses a maximum and a weak lfdr inequality under monotonicity, without a global continuity or endpoint-version condition that always guarantees attainment. Theorems 5/6 add unique interior crossings and local smoothness, avoiding an ambiguous threshold in their own setting. The empty-set convention remains tau*=0.

Assumption (iii) uses m^(1/3)(ell-hat-ell) converging to zero in probability. The additional condition (25) instead prints m^(-1/3)|ell-hat-ell| inside a tail probability. That weaker-looking exponent is preserved exactly; no expected positive exponent is substituted for it.

The source requires only P{m^(1/3)(pi-hat_0-pi_0)>epsilon}=o(m^(-2/3)), without an absolute value or a lower-tail condition. This alone does not imply two-sided consistency, despite the preceding specialization discussion. A two-sided condition is not silently imported from Theorem 5.

The explicit estimator (12) is strictly positive but may exceed one, and no clipping is specified. Theorem 6 allows any estimator under its printed one-sided condition, without separately requiring pi-hat_0>0; alpha/pi-hat_0 therefore needs a convention if it is zero. Theorem 5 likewise does not specify a domain for the random ell-hat. These omissions are recorded instead of supplying an unstated truncation.

The proofs of Theorems 4 and 5 and the asymptotic analysis are deferred to Appendix A. Only its heading crop was inspected. All objects required to state the saved Theorems are resolved from the main text; no appendix proof assumptions are imported.

value.note: The notation paragraph says a_n>>b_n means a_n/b_n tends to zero. This reverses the conventional reading used by the later signal and threshold discussion. Both the notation and original theorem inequalities are retained without choosing a correction.

The trend adds gamma_k at a break, whereas the local contrast and jump estimate subtract the right mean from the left. At an isolated positive jump their expectation has the opposite sign. Equation (20) nevertheless prints a positive tent-weighted gamma_k, and Theorem 2(iii) compares gamma-hat_k minus gamma_(k*). The disagreement is preserved.
The minimum starts at k=0 but the model only defines gamma_1,...,gamma_K. No gamma_0 convention is supplied. The original index range is not changed to make the condition well formed.

At Q_n=omega the algorithm enters its else branch but its strict-exceedance candidate set is empty, leaving max{k:A_k nonempty} undefined. Argmax and nearest-break ties have no explicit selection rule. Estimated quantities indexed up to true K also need an extension off the high-probability event K-hat=K. These omissions are not filled into source statements.

The jump estimate evaluates the left mean at tau-hat_k-bn and right mean at tau-hat_k+bn-1. These shifted windows can fall outside the observed range for candidate locations allowed by Algorithm 1. No boundary extension rule is supplied. The original shifts and subtraction order are retained.

value.note: The exact centering in (7) uses coordinate variances at a fixed index. Remark 5 approximates it by 2p/(bn); the discussion after Theorem 2 instead writes an expectation at a selected random index. These expressions are not silently identified. The extracted centering and theorem use the original bar-c definition.

The displayed covariance has an overlap indicator with a free j, and no sum over j. It also invokes Xi from (11), which already includes a factor p. This does not unambiguously define the full comparison covariance. The printed expression is retained without inferring an overlap-count correction.

The numbered definition specifies coordinate subsets, while surrounding prose describes adjacent series and uses contiguity in a window-count argument. The definition itself is retained; an arbitrary set is not silently rewritten as an interval. Assumptions 6-7 and the influenced-set construction belong to Proposition 1, not a stored Theorem.

The source simultaneously puts locations in Z^v and represents them as scaled iid vectors having a density bounded above and away from zero on [0,1]^v. No rounding or alternative ambient space is specified. The density assumption is preserved as written, rather than replaced by the separate mass-to-volume discussion. Independence of random locations from the noise is not explicitly stated.

The source calls each interval an interval on Z and then assigns its rectangle Lebesgue volume. A literal finite lattice rectangle has zero Lebesgue measure; a continuous enclosing rectangle would be a different interpretation. The source does not state that change of interpretation. Its mass comparability condition is retained with the full definition.

Equation (5) uses sigma_j squared for the long-run variance; equation (44) instead defines sigma(l)=sigma(l,l) as the variance, but later inverses and the correlation ratio use sigma(l) as if it were a standard deviation. The general formulas are preserved with no square-root correction. Unlike (5), the general setup does not explicitly repeat a uniform positive variance bound.

The nonlinear representation uses ell-prime in Z^v, but both displayed coupled versions use Z. The replacement rule is stated only for i>=0 although the process uses an entire negative-time history. The double-star rule replaces i=0 OR s=0, not only their intersection. These source domains and logical conditions are retained.

The piecewise covariance formula covers only zeta>0 and does not state its diagonal or other same-time entries. The overlap indicator requires both spatial indices in the intersection of the two rectangles, as printed. No zero-lag limit or different overlap weights are supplied by the census. The detailed evaluation is referred to appendix Lemma 15, which was not read.

Theorems 1 and 3 explicitly exclude dependence of the implicit constant on n,p,b; Theorem 4 additionally excludes S. These exact clauses are retained, as are the different error rates. The Gaussian comparison laws are finite vectors depending on the asymptotic parameters, not a single fixed limiting distribution.

The variance estimator is referred to Appendix A.1 and the detailed general covariance evaluation to Lemma 15 in Appendix C. No appendix body was inspected. The census preserves the known-scale main-text statistic and records the covariance specification omissions rather than importing those details.

The initial boundary preview incidentally included two introductory lines below the appendix heading. The retained crop was tightened to the heading only; no supplement mathematics, theorem statements or proofs were inspected or used.
Source-fidelity review does not certify proof correctness. In particular, the printed minimax test-class event conflicts with the lower bound, and remains explicitly documented.
Corollaries for particular dependence measures and proofs in the online supplement are outside the Theorem inventory. Their extra assumptions are not imported into the five saved statements.

value.note: After the supremum over the whole null class, the statement gives cases and a strictness condition in terms of theta_i of an unspecified F. The dependence of these conditions on the law over which the supremum ranges is not made precise. These are preserved as printed rather than converted to pointwise limits or different subclasses.
The model and class F use distribution functions on R^p, while the prose introducing H_0 says R^d. The parameter is in R^d. This mismatch is recorded without changing either source passage.

The normalized statistic divides by the jackknife standard error, but no convention is given for zero estimates. Assumption (A2) permits degeneracy when |theta_i| is small; Theorem 2.4 uses an alternative class imposing only (A1). The census does not silently define 0/0 or add non-degeneracy to that alternative class.

The combinatorial statistic requires enough observations and the jackknife formula requires n>m. The Gumbel constants require d>1, while the printed gamma range includes gamma=0 and does not by itself force d to diverge. These are implicit domain or regime needs, not additions to the original theorem statements.

For beta<1 the exponential function used here is not a Young function giving an ordinary norm. The source calls the quantity an Orlicz norm throughout beta in (0,2]. Its actual formula, not a different norm definition, is recorded.

The correlation condition presupposes meaningful first-projection correlations in (-1,1), whereas (A2) permits zero variances on coordinates close to zero. The sum excludes i=j, though the introductory correlation definition does not separately state that index restriction. No zero-variance correlation convention is supplied.

The source claims H_0(Delta) is contained in H_(0,boot)(Delta). The latter adds uncentered and repeated-index bounds (A1-prime), which do not follow simply from centered distinct-index bounds in (A1). The two actual class definitions are kept separate; the inclusion is not used to remove a condition.
Every value outside [-Delta,Delta] is mapped to positive Delta, including negative values. The formula is preserved; signed clipping would be a different bootstrap construction.

The prose calls q* a quantile of the bootstrap statistic’s distribution without always repeating conditional on the observations. The resampling construction and conditional mean V_i establish the conditional bootstrap law. It is not treated as an unconditional Monte Carlo quantile.

The hypothesis block assumes (A1-prime),(A2), but the displayed power infimum ranges over H_1 as defined using only (A1). The census retains that written class and separately records the theorem’s overall hypotheses; it does not silently replace the displayed class by an intersection. The bounded-kernel refinement removes only the extra logarithmic factor in the separation.

The proposed rejection formulas in (2.29),(2.32) use starred bootstrap statistics as their observed statistics. Theorem 2.8 instead explicitly uses the unstarred absolute statistic. The saved theorem follows its own printed event; the conflicting decision formula is archived separately.

The source says rejection for Delta_0 implies rejection for every Delta>Delta_0, immediately after noting the observed statistic decreases with Delta. The displayed preceding comparison points toward smaller thresholds. This remark is not an inventoried Theorem and is not used to strengthen one.

The printed test class bounds null nonrejection instead of null rejection. It therefore includes the always-reject test, for which alternative nonrejection is zero, contradicting the positive right side 1-alpha-beta in (3.3). The source definition and theorem are preserved; the audit does not certify this claim or repair the event.

The letter beta previously parameterizes Orlicz tails; Theorem 3.5 introduces beta again as a positive error allowance with alpha+beta<1. This overloading is recorded, with both source formulas unchanged. The covariance unit-variance and c_0<1-Delta conditions are specific to this theorem.

Source-fidelity and dependency validation do not certify proof correctness or repair the printed algorithms. In particular, empty-interval selection, the free polynomial index, positive dyadic bandwidths and the duplicate threshold assignment remain documented.

The complete original class paragraph is retained for both its full and conventional applications. The latter is interpreted through the paper’s explicit no-source setup, with that projection limitation stated separately.

The source labels R_C and R_I are local scalar rate definitions inside their respective upper-bound Theorems. They are archived and resolved for adaptive reuse without inventing new statistical functionals.

value.note: The main-text formulas call the noises independent and bound their uncentered absolute tails, but do not explicitly state zero means or independence between design points, curves and noises. A tail bound alone does not give mean-zero errors; these omissions can matter for identifying f^[t] from Y. The census does not supply extra assumptions or certify the rates under a repaired model.

The bounds hold for each given x with a common proxy, not for the supremum over x inside probability. Only subject/noise indices 1 and 11 are printed in the tail formulas. Subject copies are identically distributed, but identical noise laws are not stated explicitly in the observation prose. The original quantifier scope is preserved.

The prose suggests identical target and source counts, while the equations use distinct n_t,n_s,m_t,m_s. Subsequent formulas depend on their distinction. The exact equations control the recorded convention; no equalities across target and source are added.

The symbol P is introduced for the full transfer model and reused when n_s=0. The source does not separately formalize the projected law class. D17 preserves the original paragraph plus both no-source passages, and records its target-only application without importing source observations or transfer algorithms.

Omega(alpha) is the largest integer strictly below alpha. Algorithm 1 separately requires a positive integer degree, even where omega(alpha)=0. The degree constraints in both adaptive procedures still refer to unknown smoothness; a fixed known upper smoothness bound is not stated in these passages. Adaptivity is not strengthened beyond the source’s actual conditions.

M_delta first denotes a fixed supremum bound for a difference function, and later denotes a growing algorithm threshold log(n_t n_s). These roles are distinguished in the analysis while retaining the same source symbol. They are not equated as model parameters.

The source design endpoint is printed T_[m_t+1]^[s]=1 although the source gap maximum runs to m_s+1. The m_t index is retained in the original statement and inherited hypothesis archive; it is not changed to m_s.

The common bandwidths use slash notation such as ceil(m_t/2 B_t(d_t+1))^-1 without denominator parentheses. The literal typeset expressions are preserved rather than choosing a new operator grouping in the original statement.

The source requires a 1/m-packing and 1/(2m)-covering subcollection of arbitrary design points. Simultaneous existence is not established by the printed instruction, and it is not the standard maximal-packing radius pair. No replacement separation or coverage radius is substituted.

Uniform selection from each subject’s observations in each interval is undefined when that set is empty. This can occur for independent designs even under positive bounded densities, especially with the displayed small bandwidths. The later least-squares fallback does not define the preceding empty-set draw. No implicit skip rule is added.
The regression basis contains q-1 even though the interval index is r and q is not bound. Step 9 instead uses r-1. The free q is preserved and separately flagged.

The source does not specify interval endpoint assignment or a measurable tie-break among nonunique polynomial fits. It specifies zero when a solution is unavailable. Its set notation for pooled data also requires preserving multiplicities and distinct subject identities to represent K n_s subjects. These implementation conventions are recorded as unresolved, not inserted into source quotations.

The claimed max gap=o(1/m_t) is incompatible with m_t+1 nonnegative gaps summing to one. The theorem’s actual inherited bound is at most C_t/m_t. The weighted empirical loss itself sums only j=1,...,m_t and leaves the final endpoint gap out, as printed.

The estimator’s last source argument is D^[s,ell], while the experiment and rate use K source populations. Ell is not defined in this theorem. The original ell remains; the mismatch is not silently repaired.

The candidate sets use 2^r for positive r, incompatible with b in 1/Z+ required by the called base algorithm. The claimed literal inclusion of the theorem-optimal bandwidths also does not follow from a dyadic grid. Both source passages are retained.
Both assignments are to M_s: log n_s and log n_t n_s. M_delta is subsequently passed to A_TL but is not assigned by this step. The second M_s is preserved.

Theorem 3.2 requires B_t,B_delta at least Gamma_t and B_s at least Gamma_s, the upper density bounds. Algorithm 4 instead prints the lower bounds C_t,C_s. Moreover, its B constants do not appear in the candidate-grid formulas. No substitution is made.

Positive thresholds and negative powers of logarithms require suitable positive sample sizes, in particular n_t,n_s>1 where these choices are used. This fits eventual asymptotic use but is not a claim of well-definedness for every small integer sample size. Conventional n_s=0 formulas do not invoke the source-logarithm prescriptions.

Read literally, a deterministic assignment can satisfy this realized-action statement, although positivity for identifying all regimes requires support for the counterfactual actions. value.note: Adding a finite constant cannot make arbitrary integrable outcomes with unbounded negative support uniformly positive. Moreover, the source itself notes that shifting outcomes can change the hinge condition (13). Positive outcomes are retained as a model restriction where imposed, not declared irrelevant for surrogate policies.
H_2 is defined as (O_1,Y_1,O_2,A_1), while Theorem 2 writes h_2=(h_1,a_1,y_1,o_2). The ordering discrepancy is retained, with the conceptual history components identified separately.

The action space is {-1,1}, but the indicator policy formula produces {0,1}, and Theorem 4 gives htilde_n,2 an extra {0,1} factor even though H_2 already includes A_1. Neither coding nor the extra argument is silently changed.

value.note: Remark 1 fixes optimal ties to +1, whereas the eta paragraph assigns -1 otherwise after the strict >1/2 case. Theorem 2 also uses set-valued surrogate rules yet writes a_1=dtilde_1(h_1) as a scalar equality. Set membership is not substituted for the printed equality.

The strict indicators yield no reward contribution when a score is zero. The following prose permits either action at zero, which need not match that formula for positive rewards. The original formula and tie claims are both preserved.

The source writes V_psi* through an extended-valued maximizer, then explicitly says Definition 1 does not require such maximizers to exist or be measurable. The corresponding supremum is recorded as the interpretation of the optimum; no attainment assumption is added to Fisher consistency.

The printed strict-concavity inequality quantifies all x,y in the effective domain without excluding x=y, making the literal inequality impossible at a repeated point. The original passage is saved, and the usual distinct-point restriction is not inserted into it.

The first branch is stated at h_1, but its failure conclusion uses capital H_1. The theorem does not specify how to choose a surrogate maximizer jointly across histories before stating all stagewise alternatives. The exact h_1/H_1 and scalar/set notation are retained.

The paper uses min(x-1,y-1,0), a figure caption max(x-1,y-1,0), and the Theorem 2 function min(x,y,1). The source’s shift discussion claims the two sides of (13) increase by C and 3C; substituting Y_1+C,Y_2+C instead leaves the contrast unchanged and adds 4C to the reward sum. These prose claims are not used to alter Theorem 2.

Condition 2 requires strict increase, positivity, reflected sum and limits, but does not require continuity or a derivative. Types A/B add differentiability away from zero. The theorem graphs keep these as separate requirements despite the source’s smoothed-loss terminology.

The final phrase says all t<t_0 without explicitly restricting t>0, although arbitrary positive real exponents are used. The intended small positive radius interpretation is recorded separately; the original t range is preserved. The exclusion of equality at the boundary permits atoms there.

The claimed equivalent contrast formulation drops absolute values and only controls positive small contrasts, whereas B controls both sides around one half. The saved theorem dependencies use B itself rather than this differing formula.

The condition literally bounds eta_1 and eta_2 away from zero. Decision boundaries occur at eta_t=1/2, so this does not imply the separation claimed in the surrounding prose and is not equivalent to an infinite noise exponent. Theorems 6/7 retain the literal source assumption without correction.

The later value display replaces fhat_t by phi(fhat_t) inside sign indicators. Under Condition 2 this always chooses positive actions, unlike the original value definition (5). The conflicting display is archived as A10; it is not substituted for the original definition.

Several sentences call V_psi(fhat) the psi-regret and V(fhat) the true regret, omitting the optimal-value subtraction. The original regret definitions and the actual theorem inequalities retain the subtraction. The informal wording does not redefine those quantities.

The informal class-approximation claim (20) omits scaling by a_n. Theorem 4 bounds scaled scores; Theorem 5 assumes explicitly that approximants in U_n divided by a_n are close to eta_t-1/2. No unstated scaling closure of U_n is added.

Theorem 5 does not explicitly impose the derivative-tail types A/B used in Theorem 4, while Condition 2 alone supplies no quantitative tail approach to its limits. The source scope is preserved with Condition 2 only; no proof-derived derivative condition is added to make the displayed rate easier to justify.

The source calls N the bracketing entropy but defines a number of brackets. Theorems 5/7 bound N, whereas (23) for Theorem 6 bounds log N with exponent 2rho_n. The metrics also differ; these conditions are not merged.

Bounds involving L2(P_n) depend on the observed sample. The main text does not state whether these inequalities are deterministic over all samples, almost sure, or on a specified event, nor an explicit epsilon range or uniformity of the implicit constants. These quantifier omissions are retained as unresolved.

The bracketing definition is for scalar functions, while (24) uses the pair class U_n with L2(P_n). The source does not specify a pair norm or identify the induced scalar loss class here. The formula is preserved without replacing U_n by its coordinate classes or a loss class.

Theorem 4 binds a_n tending to infinity but only calls delta_n a small number; it does not explicitly require delta_n to tend to zero. In Theorems 5-7 the probability guarantee is stated for each n,x, not as one event simultaneously covering all n,x. Uniformity of constants over varying rho_n, A_n and distributions is not fully specified.

Theorem 1’s extra script-I membership and Theorem 4’s unparenthesized chi_p expression/equality chain remain exactly as printed. Source fidelity is not a certification of those statements as mathematically well posed.

Appendix and supplement references remain references. Proof-only expansions, the later adaptive-delta algorithm, empirical bootstrap variance estimation and applied confidence regions do not become theorem statement requirements.
Fixed s in Theorems 1/2, dimension p in Theorem 3 and growing sparse-support size s in Theorem 4 remain distinct.

Natural-language group titles use source keywords. Shared component grouping does not rewrite any original definition or claim mathematical equivalence between moments, estimators and variance quantities.

value.description: Theorem 1 prints (alpha,beta) in script I in M(gamma;C_1). Script I denotes the edge-index set on page 4. This is an ill-typed or typographical membership chain, not a silently corrected hypothesis. Theorem 2 refers to the conditions of Theorem 1 and inherits this unresolved source wording.

Theorem 4 prints exp(-|xi^+| vee max_S |check-theta^+|) without grouping the maximum under the minus sign. Its intended negative-maximum interpretation is suggested by the subsequent chi_p^-1 discussion, but the original theorem formula is not repaired.

Theorem 4 writes the same rate expression as a literal equality between the intercept error and the maximum sparse-effect error. The preceding triangle inequalities justify bounds, not equality of those random errors. The printed chain is retained.

The source defines tilde-O_p through some sufficiently small fixed positive epsilon and a factor p^epsilon. It neither means only logarithmic factors nor explicitly quantifies every epsilon. This nonstandard convention is preserved.

The original and bootstrap moment estimators use logarithms of empirical ratios that may be zero, negative or undefined on finite-sample outcomes. No measurable fallback or truncation is specified. Asymptotic rates do not themselves define the estimator on all outcomes.

Noise variables are described as independent (and bootstrap noises iid), but independence from the original graph or the first sanitized graph is not separately stated. The conditional-flip identities and population-moment identities use fresh release noise. This implicit kernel interpretation is documented rather than added to quoted source statements.

The class M uses C_1<alpha,beta<0.5 and gamma=1-alpha-beta. It is empty when gamma>=1-2C_1, despite stating the nominal range gamma in (0,1]. The unnoised gamma=1 case discussed in remarks is outside this class.

Theorem 2 refers to the conditions of Theorem 1. Its own gamma window ranges across the three alternative phase branches; these branches are not simultaneous hypotheses. No Theorem-1 conclusion is imported as a new statement dependency.

Theorem 2 is printed as convergence of theta-hat-dagger centered at theta and normalized by population nu-dagger. It is not a conditional bootstrap theorem centered at theta-hat. Theorem 3 uses theta-hat and population V-dagger. The later Monte Carlo variance estimate is a different object.

The sparse model uses R_+^p together with a zero minimum, so nonnegativity must include zero here. Its residual parameters can be signed. The source does not define max over an empty support, although the sparsity conditions alone allow empty support.

The norm display following (6.2) omits the inactive coordinates xi/2. In particular it claims o(log p) when omega_1=2omega_2, even though omega_1>0 and inactive nodes yield order log p. This asserted identity is not treated as a separate definition or condition.

Theorem 4 does not assume the dense-model Condition 1 or give a sparse bootstrap central limit theorem. The preceding section explicitly describes a limited sparse extension. Dense assumptions and bootstrap variance interfaces are excluded from its dependency closure.
The sparse estimates in (6.3) are unthresholded. They are not constrained to be nonnegative or to have support S, and the theorem does not promise support recovery.

Theorems 1/2 keep s fixed as p grows. Theorem 3 is p-dimensional. Theorem 4 uses s as the size of a potentially growing sparse support with s=o(p). These quantifiers are distinct despite reusing the letter s.

Inverse square roots of variance terms and triangle averaging require positive normalizations and p>=3. These hold eventually under the interior model restrictions for the intended population quantities, but the source does not supply arbitrary-value conventions for excluded finite cases.
Theorem 4 uses M(gamma,C_1) with a comma, whereas the class definition uses a semicolon. The same class is resolved from Section 3.3 while the printed theorem punctuation remains unchanged.

Definition 1 takes a supremum only where the denominator Q(Z|X)>0. For general kernels with unequal supports, this does not expressly compare the omitted zero-denominator case; the census retains the exact definition. The interior jittering kernel used by the Theorems has common full support.

References to proofs and variance estimates in the Appendix or embedded supplement were not followed. The pinned source is arXiv v2; equality of its statements to final journal wording has not been established.

value: Main-text source transcription and statement-dependency review; no proof certification or silent source repairs.
All appendix and supplement mathematics were excluded.
The source is the published journal paper, not a preprint. Main-text source fidelity does not certify correctness of its proofs or resolve its apparent typographical errors.
Algorithm 4’s population S-star_jj, Assumption 3’s var(E_ij squared), the rectangular noise-index mismatch and Theorem 5’s starred iteration parameter are preserved and explained separately.
The Gaussian signal statement is retained. Footnote 1’s unrestricted sub-Gaussian extension is archived without asserting unchanged fourth-moment-sensitive covariance-entry variance formulas.
Definition 1 and Assumption 2 remain distinct, as do the two noise models, condition numbers and HeteroPCA scalings. No conditions are transferred through proof-only use of Theorem 5.
No appendix or supplement was opened. Generalized supplement Theorems 11-14, external proof references and comparison results are excluded from the main-text inventory.

value.description: Algorithm 4 retains omega_i^2 S-star_jj in its off-diagonal plug-in variance formula, while the paired term uses S_ii without a star. S-star_jj is not an available input. The printed procedure is therefore not fully data-driven in that branch; the census preserves this instead of substituting S_jj.

Assumption 3 prints var(E_ij^2)=sigma_ij^2 rather than var(E_ij). Equation (6.7) subsequently treats sigma_ij^2 as ordinary entry variance. This mismatch is retained without changing the assumption or certifying the resulting Theorem 5.

Theorem 5’s iteration count uses sigma_1 with a star superscript, even though the entire general-subspace model and all other singular values use natural superscripts. The source does not identify this starred quantity in Section 6; the likely typo is not repaired or used to import the PCA model.

The general model prints E=[E_ij] with both indices in [n], but M and M-natural are n_1 by n_2, and Assumption 3 has the rectangular index range. The source dimensional mismatch is preserved; the intended rectangular perturbation is stated separately in the interpretation.

The Gaussian-signal footnote asserts that all results extend to isotropic sub-Gaussian factors without specifying fourth-moment matching or modified variances. Covariance-entry fluctuations generally depend on these fourth moments. The Gaussian theorem statements remain authoritative, with the broader footnote archived separately.

The model independently specifies Gaussian columns, sampling indicators and noise entries, without explicitly asserting joint independence of the three collections. The conditional Gram expectation (2.2) uses that intended independence. It is documented as implicit model context, not inserted into original quotations.

Assumption 1 uses omega_max squared divided by omega_min squared. A finite ratio excludes a zero minimum when some row noise is positive; the all-zero 0/0 case has no printed convention. The census does not silently add noiseless cases to the inferential theorems.

The matrix-sign function is defined only for nonsingular H. Theorems 1/2 use H=U^T U-star, with no explicit rule at singular outcomes or eigenvector ties. A high-probability nonsingularity argument does not supply a total finite-sample definition.

Algorithms 2 and 5 use a loop t=0,...,t_0 and output quantities at t_0, after also computing G at t_0+1. This indexing is preserved. Both algorithms leave eigenvalue tie breaking, rank-r spectral selection details and square roots of nonpositive eigenvalues unspecified.

Algorithms 3/4 divide by the number of observed entries in a row and subtract S_ll to estimate a variance. Empty rows and negative variance estimates have no stated fallback. Estimated covariance square roots, inverse Sigma and scalar variance square roots can therefore be undefined on some finite-sample outcomes.
Algorithm 3 adds a row U_l to Sigma_U,l^(1/2) z written as a column-vector transformation. The source implicitly identifies row and column representations of R^r; the original expression is retained.

Theorem 2 bounds the largest marginal rowwise coverage error. It does not assert that all d row regions simultaneously cover with probability 1-alpha. Theorem 4 is likewise an entrywise statement, not simultaneous coverage of all matrix entries.

Theorem 1 says for all l and gives an o(1) convex-set error, while Theorem 2 explicitly places a supremum over l outside the coverage error. These printed quantifier forms are preserved rather than replaced by a single simultaneous-event claim.

Theorem 3 assumes ndp^2 at least a log^7 scale; Theorem 4 increases this to log^8. Theorem 1’s distinct log^9 requirement is not inherited by Theorem 3, despite nearby interpretive prose referring to conditions of Theorem 1.

The paper defines << as a sufficiently small constant-factor inequality. It does not mean little-o. Theorem 5’s zeta_op condition must retain this source meaning, and the constants in the other comparison symbols are not assigned numerical values.

The covariance model’s kappa is a ratio of eigenvalues, while kappa-natural in Section 6 is a ratio of singular values. Likewise n is the PCA sample count in Sections 1-3 and max(n_1,n_2) in Section 6. The two meanings are not merged.

Definition 1 has one eigenspace row-norm condition. Assumption 2 has left and right singular-space row bounds plus an entrywise signal bound. Assumption 3 is bounded-noise and does not require PCA’s finite heteroskedasticity ratio. These distinct conditions are not transferred across models.

Section 6 prints sigma_r-natural>=0 although it describes an exact rank-r matrix and uses its reciprocal. Exact rank r is the intended positive-singular-value setting; zero-rank or zero-denominator conventions are not supplied.

Algorithms 3/4 use a coverage input 1-alpha and quantiles, but the theorem statements do not separately quantify alpha or uniformity over varying alpha. Ordinary fixed 0<alpha<1 confidence levels are the interpretation; uniform shrinking-tail coverage is not asserted.

Theorem 5 gives an existential pair Z,Psi on an event of probability exceeding 1-O(n^-10), followed by all-row bounds. Its explicit formula fixes Z and the decomposition fixes Psi. It is not a conditional Gaussian theorem and does not depend on the PCA Gaussian-column assumption.

The orthogonal Procrustes argmin is written as a single matrix in (6.9), with no selection rule for multiple minimizers. The orthonormal matrix set includes reflections; no determinant-one constraint is stated.

Proof expansions in Section 3.3 and Appendix references do not become statement dependencies. The main-paper reference to Theorems 11-14 in the separate supplement does not create additional inventoried theorems. No supplement body was opened.

The unrestricted h formulation of strong negative type, median-separation formula versus prose, profile-anchor mismatch, scalar-rank extra argument, permutation split index and estimated-CDF subscript remain source issues rather than corrected quotations.

The source does not fully specify nonnegativity of weights, the covariance eigenvalue operator, global density/support continuity, probability over composite alternatives or all quantile endpoint conventions. These limitations are preserved in the source-convention record.
The census includes every main-text result labeled Theorem. Proposition 1, examples, simulation claims, discussion assertions and all embedded supplement results remain outside that inventory.

value.description: The first strong-negative-type formulation quantifies over all measurable h, omitting a mean-zero and integrability restriction. It is not equivalent as printed to (9): for a point-mass P the zero diagonal kernel makes the quadratic form zero for every h, contradicting its equality-only-if-h=0 clause. Both formulations are transcribed literally.

Section 3 discusses strong negative type for a powered distance d^theta, but Theorem 4.1(d) invokes the metric space (Omega,d) itself. A property of an arbitrary other power is not substituted for the theorem hypothesis; Proposition 1 is a distinct result type and is not added to the Theorem inventory.

Assumption 2 asks for a continuous density and a strictly positive infimum over its support. With the usual global continuity and support conventions, this is problematic at the boundary of a bounded nonnegative distance distribution. The source may intend continuity on the interior, but this is not specified and is not repaired.

Assumption 3 takes the infimum outside each individual median’s epsilon ball. If there were two distinct medians, choosing epsilon below their distance would make the rank gap zero. Its prose describes separated multiple medians, which does not agree with the formula. The census retains the formula instead of changing it to separation from the entire median set.
Theorem 4.1(c) writes R_gamma(s)(u) and R_gamma(t)(u), although (12) defines scalar ranks with no u argument. This extra argument is preserved in the theorem and recorded separately.

Equation (22) indexes profiles by omega but writes d(x,X) and d(x,Y), leaving x unbound in that sentence. The intended anchor interpretation is clear from (8) and Assumption 5, but the original equation is retained.

The permutation split gives Y_Pi_j the second entry V_Pi_j(2), overlapping the first group, instead of the expected V_Pi_j(n+2). Its literal formula conflicts with the accompanying claim of splitting into two groups of sizes n and m. No corrected algorithm is silently substituted.

Assumption 4 does not require nonnegative weights. Theorem 6.1 nevertheless uses sqrt(w_x(u)w_x(v)) and a chi-square-series law. Negative or sign-changing weights create a mismatch between the statistic and that representation; the positivity imposed for identification after (26) is not explicitly repeated in Assumption 4. The missing condition is flagged, not inserted.

Theorem 6.1 calls lambda_j^x the eigenvalues of a covariance surface without explicitly specifying the associated operator space or integration measure. The literal averaged pointwise eigenvalue series is preserved; no alternative covariance operator or spectral formula is inferred from a proof.

The source calls H_nm contiguous alternatives but defines only D=a_nm tending to zero with nm/(n+m)*a_nm tending to infinity. This is not by itself a statement of Le Cam contiguity, and the source term is not expanded into that stronger probabilistic claim.

The notation P_Hnm does not state whether power is evaluated along an arbitrary chosen pair sequence or uniformly over the composite set. The source also uses a null-law critical value under alternatives without specifying a particular null P there. No minimax, supremum or uniformity convention is supplied by the census.

Section 3 assumes total boundedness and separability, while Theorem 4.1 restates only separability. Total boundedness makes the rank quantile integrals finite. Extending that theorem to arbitrary unbounded separable spaces would need an integrability convention, which the local statement does not supply.

The notation F-hat_Xi denotes a leave-one-out CDF in the empirical rank formula, whereas F-hat_omega is the full-sample empirical CDF. When omega is an observation these roles coincide symbolically but differ in denominator; the two source conventions remain separate.

Assumption 2 explicitly asks for continuous densities; Assumption 5 asks for absolutely continuous profiles and densities but does not explicitly demand density continuity. Both have anchorwise positive lower bounds and uniform upper bounds. They are not merged into a stronger common condition.

Theorem 5.1 states weak convergence of the indexed process without naming a function-space topology. The preceding discussion calls the ball-indicator class P-Donsker, suggesting the usual empirical-process interpretation; this is interpretation, not extra original theorem wording.

The generalized inverse is defined on (0,1), while the map F_X inverse composed with F_omega can reach 0 or 1. Endpoint conventions are not provided. Endpoint values do not affect the rank’s Lebesgue integral, but the pointwise map is not automatically defined everywhere.

The text permits any strictly monotone invertible map from R to [0,1] after using expit with range (0,1). A decreasing transform reverses the ranking and closed-endpoint bijectivity differs from the logistic map. All theorem interpretations retain the actual expit definition, not the unrestricted prose generalization.

Total boundedness does not imply compactness. Theorem 5.3 explicitly assumes a nonempty population median set; no existence theorem or arbitrary selection rule is added. The empirical set retains all sample maximizers, and its leave-one-out rank needs n>=2.

Theorem 6.3 writes Gamma-hat_m,n rather than Gamma-hat_nm from (27). The first conclusion is pointwise at continuity points, not uniform in t. Its final power clause does not repeat K tending to infinity although the earlier permutation clauses do; this omission and the source sequence of clauses are preserved.

The two root-total-size sample-balance bounds in Theorem 6.3 are algebraically redundant, but both are retained. The mixture definition initially allows c in [0,1]; Assumption 6 restricts the theorem regime to c in (0,1).

The permutation statistic is defined by evaluating the same statistic functional on each permuted sample. No separate rule says to freeze data-adaptive weights fitted to the original group labels. The census preserves the functional definition without inventing a shortcut or an implementation.

The three critical values have different reference laws: q_alpha uses the null law, q-hat_alpha the permutation empirical CDF, and q-bar_alpha the mixture limit. The mixture quantile restricts the infimum to t>=0, while the other two do not. These definitions and their continuity hypotheses remain distinct.

The lower bound concerns a broader model than the upper-bound guarantee. The two are not reported as a uniform matching result under only the lower-bound assumptions.

The Q-hat polynomial argument, transformed-measure normalization, Euclidean-ball versus cube domain, density-ratio lower-bound wording and maximum grouping remain unresolved source conventions; quotations are not repaired.

Omega’s population Gram interpretation follows the main-text projection formula; a standalone printed Gram definition and a fully specified nuisance-estimation implementation are not supplied in the inspected text.

value.description: The strict floor in the Hölder definition is the largest integer strictly smaller than s, so at an integer s it equals s-1. This convention also fixes the degree and dimension of the Legendre basis; the usual floor at integers is not substituted.

The lower-bound model bounds the covariate density only from above. It does not explicitly require positivity near x_0 or treatment overlap. Conditional regression versions can then be unidentified at some points. Theorem 2 adds overlap and matrix conditions; these are not transferred to Theorem 1.

The text calls gamma necessarily at least beta and later repeats gamma>=beta, but the two theorem statements do not separately list this ordering. The displayed lower-bound model constrains mu_0 and tau independently. The intended regime in the prose is recorded without inventing an extra original hypothesis.

The vector norm is defined as Euclidean, so the kernel and localized-basis indicators select a ball. Later prose describes stretching a cube, and the estimated Gram integral explicitly runs over [0,1]^d. A later convention restricts v integrals to a Euclidean ball inside that cube. These differing domains are retained, not silently reconciled by using a sup norm.

F-star is written dF(x_0+h(v-1/2)) and called a local distribution, with no explicit normalization. For an ordinary bounded density, the literal restricted pushforward has mass of order h^d, while the change-of-variable formulas with K_h and the assumed eigenvalue scales suggest a rescaled interpretation. No missing h^-d factor or conditional-probability normalization is inserted.

Definition 2’s Q-hat U-statistic term ends in rho_h(X_1)^T, but equation (9) in the bias calculation uses rho_h(X_2)^T. These are different kernels. The definition and theorem reference retain the printed estimator; the discrepancy is documented separately.

The first-order treatment correction is A(A-pi-hat), not (A-pi-hat)^2. The first-order outcome correction uses the control regression mu_0, not the marginal regression eta. Familiar R-learner formulas are not substituted for these specific source formulas.

The main text displays Omega-hat explicitly and uses Omega in the coordinate formula for the F-star-weighted linear projection. It does not separately display Omega=integral bb^T dF-star. Identifying Omega as the population Gram matrix is a source-backed interpretation of that projection formula, not a verbatim extra definition.

The norm of dF-hat-star/dF-star is said to be bounded above and below away from zero. A lower bound on this sup norm does not imply a pointwise lower bound on the density ratio. The theorem’s literal condition is retained, without strengthening it to mutual domination.

Condition 1 and equation (15) print 1+d/(2gamma)+d/(4s) vee (1+d/(2gamma)) without parentheses identifying the two arguments of the maximum. Interpreting only d/(4s) versus 1+d/(2gamma) as the maximum makes the expression agree with the piecewise rates; taking the entire preceding sum as one operand does not. Both the ambiguous formula and the unambiguous piecewise conclusion are preserved.

Condition 1 divides by the product of nuisance-error norms, which can be zero. No zero-denominator convention is given. The product remainder in Remark 11 supplies an interpretation but is not substituted for the theorem’s original fraction.

Condition 1 uses a fixed-factor less-than comparison. Remark 11 describes the third-order remainder as smaller order, which is stronger if read as little-o. The comparison symbols retain their explicit Section 2 meanings.

The nuisance estimators are trained on D^n independently of the sample used by U_n, and the empirical and U-statistic terms use the common evaluation sample. The source gives no cross-fitting or ensemble averaging rule and does not state a separate training-size asymptotic. No such procedure is added.

Remark 8 expressly says that an ordinary empirical covariate distribution need not make Omega-hat invertible at the chosen k. The high-level theorem does not construct nuisance estimators satisfying every condition. The census records its required inputs, rather than claiming an unconditional ready-to-run estimator.

The estimator uses inverse Q-hat and inverse Omega-hat with no finite-sample singularity fallback. Condition C contains an inverse-error bound, implicitly requiring that inverse to exist; density-ratio norm bounds alone do not specify an estimator regularization rule.

Theorem 2 states boundedness conditions on random nuisance quantities without explicitly saying whether they hold surely, with high probability, or conditionally. Its conclusion is an expectation bound. No high-probability-only condition or unmentioned tail/uniform-integrability condition is supplied.

F-star norm expressions in the theorem use unstarred nuisance functions, whereas the main-text calculation defines stretched versions g-star(v)=g(x_0+h(v-1/2)). This suppressed composition and the h-dependent measure must be kept visible for subsequent formalization.

The polynomial basis has total-degree dimension choose(d+strict-floor(gamma),strict-floor(gamma)), not the full tensor-product dimension (strict-floor(gamma)+1)^d. The correction basis has a separate increasing dimension k. The two bases and their population matrices are not merged.

The tuning notation tilde is defined as proportionality, while k is a basis dimension and must be an integer. The source does not specify integer rounding. The strict low-smoothness branch and otherwise branch include the elbow equality exactly as printed.

The lower bound has an infimum over estimators and supremum over the broad model. The upper bound lacks that supremum and adds distribution-estimation and regularity assumptions. Remark 2 explicitly limits matching to a more restricted submodel whose appendix details are excluded.

The observed regression contrast is defined without counterfactual variables. Consistency, positivity and no unmeasured confounding identify it as a causal effect in the introduction; these are not all automatically statistical prerequisites of the lower bound.

Remark 1 discusses replacing control-regression smoothness by marginal-regression smoothness and changing s to min(alpha,s), but the actual results for that model are in Appendix A. This alternative model is not substituted into the two inventoried main-text Theorems.

Theorem 2’s reference to condition (6) is the displayed Hölder approximation property, not Proposition 6. Main-text propositions used in the proof are not additional inventoried Theorems or automatically imported assumptions. Remark 10 repeatedly calls A-C Condition 2, and Proposition 6 refers to its own assumptions; these reference defects do not change the theorem’s explicit list.

The arbitrary-family minimum in Theorem 3.2 is over an uncountable index family. Its measurability is not automatic from the stated individual-test assumptions. The predictable finite-prefix case is kept separate.
Almost-sure comparisons across uncountably many subsets need a simultaneous-version interpretation for the closure reduction; the source does not state that convention explicitly.

The two predictability definitions, adaptedness, marginal p-value validity and intersection-test level control are different requirements. No independence or past-only threshold condition is silently added.

value.description: The first assertion of Theorem 3.2 minimizes over all subsets I of N containing i, an uncountable family. An uncountable infimum of individually measurable binary tests need not be measurable. The source does not state a common measurability or outer-probability convention for this arbitrary-family closure. The predictable case has a finite-prefix reduction, but that extra premise is not inserted into the first assertion.

Section 2 interprets random-variable equalities and inequalities almost surely for every model law. The predictability definitions compare uncountably many intersections, so separate almost-sure comparisons need not have a common full-measure event. The finite-prefix reduction requires a simultaneous interpretation or consistent versions; the source does not explicitly resolve this distinction.

Theorem 3.5 writes max{d_i:i in I} for every I, including the empty set. Section 3 explicitly fixes phi_empty=0, supplying the intended empty-maximum convention. For a nonempty infinite subset the binary maximum is well defined; no real-valued compactness assumption is needed.

Online intersection tests use F_sup(I), with F_infinity=A. The empty set has no explicitly defined supremum or F_0, but its test is the separately fixed constant zero. This is not replaced by an unstated time-zero filtration definition.

An online test is only a measurability property. Its alpha-level property is a separate probability bound, and predictability is a third, across-intersection property. None is inferred automatically from the others in the census.

Definition 3.1 adds only future indices to a finite prefix intersection. It does not require rejection to persist when omitted earlier indices are inserted, and it is not the standard stochastic-process notion of predictability.

Definition 4.1 requires equality of existing thresholds when future indices are added. Definition 3.1 requires only persistence of rejection. The source explicitly says the threshold condition is stronger; the two are kept as different interfaces and are not merged.

Online alpha-adjustments are allowed to be measurable with respect to F_i, not only F_{i-1}. Thus they may depend on the current p-value. Marginally valid p-values alone do not give error control for arbitrary such thresholds; Theorem 4.2 expressly assumes level-alpha intersection tests.

The general results do not assume independent p-values, conditional superuniformity, or a filtration generated solely by previous p-values. Those assumptions appear only in explanatory examples. Theorem 4.2’s explicit intersection-test level condition remains the controlling hypothesis.

The recursion I_i in both shortcut theorems selects a random finite subset of {1,...,i}. Evaluation of phi_{I_i} or alpha_i^{I_i} uses the relevant finite-valued selection; it is not an evaluation at a fixed deterministic subset. The second theorem uses p_j>alpha_j^{I_j}, whereas the first uses phi_{I_j}=0, and both recursions are preserved literally.

Equality of procedure decisions is interpreted almost surely under each model law by the standing convention. Since the decision coordinates are countable, coordinatewise equalities can be made simultaneous per law. This is stronger than merely having the same distribution and distinct from a common event across all laws or all uncountably indexed tests.

Strong FWER is required for every model law and over the entire sequence. The increasing count v_P can equal infinity; the error event remains v_P>0. Weak global-null control is not substituted for strong control, including where Theorem 3.5 abbreviates the terminology.

The model treats each hypothesis as a subset of a fixed abstract family of probability laws. The introduction’s emphasis on hypotheses not being known in advance does not by itself define arbitrary data-dependent random hypotheses or permit selection without accounting for validity.

Consonance supplies a witness inside each rejected intersection whose containing sub-intersections are rejected. It does not impose rejection of arbitrary supersets. A raw intersection rejection is not silently identified with a rejection by every superset in the closed procedure.

The shortcut theorem gives one selected intersection test for each individual decision. It does not specify the computational cost of evaluating an arbitrary intersection test or guarantee constant-time updates for every possible family.

Individual thresholds lie in [0,1), and the decision uses a non-strict p_i<=alpha_i comparison. Non-rejections in Theorem 4.2 use the strict complement p_j>alpha_j^{I_j}; threshold equality is not reassigned to acceptance.

Theorem 3.5 is in the admissibility section but assumes no admissibility hypothesis. Definition 3.4 and later admissibility Propositions/Corollaries are not necessary statement prerequisites. Alpha-Spending, Online-Graph and ADDIS rules later instantiate the general framework but are not parameters required to state any of the four inventoried Theorems.

value.description: Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 explicitly minimize approximate objectives (22)/(23), while the full estimators in (15) minimize (12)/(14) and the surrounding prose says these full objectives are used in practice. The census does not silently assert identical minimizers or transfer a theorem between them.

The parameter search space in Section 2 is the closure of the product of bounded open convex domains. The true parameter is interior. In contrast, the forward-flow domain, semigroup quantifier and (A6) on page 8 use unbarred Theta_beta. The different printed domains are retained; inverse availability at every boundary search parameter is not asserted.

The initial parameter is (beta,Sigma), the consistency target is (beta,Sigma Sigma^T), and the normality coordinates are (beta,varsigma). The paper explains covariance identifiability but does not explicitly redefine Theta under these coordinate changes. A parameter domain for a future implementation needs to respect this distinction.

The shorthand Sigma Sigma_0^T means the true covariance Sigma_0 Sigma_0^T, not a product of a candidate Sigma with the true transpose. Derivatives of F_0 and the true covariance in (27) are interpreted as differentiating the family before evaluation at the true parameter.

Assumption (A6) says the inverse is defined asymptotically for all x and beta when h tends to zero. It does not specify a uniform small-step threshold over states and parameters, or a global inverse for every finite h. The source itself acknowledges possible nonexistence within the optimization search domain.

Corollary 3.8 proof invokes polynomial growth of the inverse flow. That extra inverse-growth statement is not explicit in (A6). The census preserves (A6) rather than adding this proof claim as a new theorem hypothesis.

The inverse-Jacobian identity printed on page 10 evaluates the forward and inverse Jacobians at the same x. The general inverse-function identity evaluates the forward Jacobian at f_h^{-1}(x). The source formula is archived unchanged and not treated as a verified algebraic identity.

The OU covariance expansion (6) literally ends with the weaker matrix remainder R(h,x_0) after its h and h^2 terms. It is not transcribed as R(h^3,x_0), even though a stronger order is natural from the integral formula.

R is defined for a first argument in (0,1), with polynomial state dependence and an unspecified constant. Theorems use it as order notation, not a fixed common function. The approximate-objective introduction also writes R(Nh^2,x_0), while consistency alone assumes h to zero and Nh to infinity, without Nh^2 to zero.

Strong Lp errors compare paths, so the OU innovations must be coupled to the driving Wiener increments. The source identifies them through the OU flow and states their iid Gaussian law; a distribution-only construction with unrelated independent noise would not preserve the strong comparison.

The grid has N increments and N+1 observations, with T=Nh. Numerical moment/error bounds are on a finite horizon; the estimation Theorems explicitly let the observation horizon diverge. The census does not assume every numerical-bound constant is uniform in a growing horizon.

Definition 3.1 uses a conditional mean error of order q1 and a conditional 2p-moment root of order q2, with q1 at least q2+1/2. Theorem 3.3 uses 2p moments for p>=1; Theorems 3.5 and 3.7 use p moments for p>=2. The printed existential C>=1 is retained even though C does not explicitly occur in the displayed conclusions.

Assumption (A1) explicitly gives C2 regularity for N, while Section 2 only describes A and b as parameterized functions and F as locally Lipschitz. The information matrix needs parameter derivatives of F. The source extraction does not silently add a separate smoothness assumption on A and b.

Assumption (A3) states existence of an invariant probability. It does not itself explicitly assert uniqueness, ergodicity, stationary initialization, or all invariant moments. Assumption (A5) states equality of drifts for every state, not merely almost everywhere under that probability.

Section 2 assumes positive-definite covariance and the estimation Theorems explicitly include (A4). Prose discusses the potential applicability of S to hypoelliptic models, with proofs deferred to a separate paper. Those extensions are not added to the scope of the printed Theorems.

The source vech ordering is S_11,S_12,S_22,...,S_1d,...,S_dd. It must not be replaced by a different triangular ordering without coordinating derivatives and information blocks. For a diagonal covariance the source uses diag instead; its dimension is d rather than the general s=d(d+1)/2.

The source Jacobian convention puts derivative index first. Transposition does not alter the trace used in (23), but the convention should not be silently replaced when interpreting other matrix products. The census records the original definition separately.

The statement minimizers are not accompanied by explicit existence, measurable-selection, tie-breaking or failed-inverse-domain conventions. These are unresolved implementation choices, not extra conditions inserted into the original Theorems.

Theorems 3.3 and 3.5 repeat cited external results but are nevertheless printed as Theorems in the main text and are included. Lemmas, Propositions and Corollaries remain outside the inventory; no supplementary proofs or code have been opened.
