value.description: Theorems 4.2 and 6.1 require B4-B6, whose definitions are explicitly placed in Appendix B. The main text only describes their purpose. Their exact content remains unresolved because appendix mathematics is excluded; no synthesized assumption is substituted.

A1 requires coordinatewise maps to be injective and measurable. The next page calls the requirements bijective. Surjectivity and measurable inverse on the image are not explicit in A1. The pushforward notation itself means preimage, but recovering the original Gibbs dynamics needs an appropriate measurable correspondence.

Section 2 starts with an unspecified common product space. Regular conditional distributions and a measurable inverse of an injective map are not automatic on arbitrary measurable spaces. The paper does not explicitly impose standard-Borel spaces here; the Euclidean applications have a more concrete framework.

The targets depend on data, and convergence in A1 is under Q^(n). The statement of A1 does not spell out measurability conventions for data-dependent transformations or the supremum over warm starts. The census retains the probability assertion without promoting it to a deterministic statement.

The coordinate-update display says i=1,...,n even though the immediately preceding text and product kernel use K coordinates. The original display is retained and the indexing discrepancy is recorded separately.

Theorem 2.4 holds for each fixed t and fixed M. It does not claim a bound uniform in time, convergence from every point mass, or convergence of spectral gaps. The source explicitly distinguishes these stronger claims.

The source calls the distance a total variation norm but does not give a normalization formula in the relevant main-text definitions. All literal inequalities and epsilon thresholds are retained. A future implementation should fix the normalization consistently rather than silently switching between variation norm and probability total variation distance.

The infimum in (4) and the hierarchical mixing definition begins at t>=0, whereas the limiting mixing definition on page 7 begins at t>=1. Iterations are discrete because they are powers of a Markov kernel. The empty infimum convention is infinity, and the threshold comparison is strictly less than epsilon.

Warm starts are measure domination on measurable events, not closeness in total variation. Theorem 4.2 uses a fixed M and worst-case initialization; Theorem 6.1 replaces it with the explicit data-dependent law (35) and does not state a fixed deterministic M-warm bound.

Theorem 3.1 assumes correct iid specification, injective likelihood parameterization, square-root density regularity, local prior absolute continuity and positivity, and two explicit testing limits. None of these is replaced by a generic invocation of Bernstein-von Mises. The Gaussian mean contains the random score term I^{-1}Delta and is not zero for its stated transformation.

In the f-model discussion the source prints X in R^K rather than a subset relation and misspells continously. Both are preserved in the original passages. The Fisher information symbol is calligraphic I, and the Gaussian law is ordinary N, not the calligraphic warm-start class N.

The hierarchical local prior is assumed exponential-family with the source’s linear-independence description of minimality. The likelihood is allowed to be arbitrary under domination and later B-conditions; no exponential-family likelihood or global prior is assumed.

B2 uses lower-case j in u_j while its domain and limiting index use upper-case J. It also writes dy integrals over R^(mJ), although Section 4 permits a counting or other sigma-finite dominating measure. These notational choices remain literal, with the reference-measure interpretation recorded separately.

The expectation defining marginal Fisher information has no parameter subscript. Its conventional interpretation is under g(.;psi). This matrix is distinct from the f-model information in Theorem 3.1 even though the same calligraphic symbol is used.

Theorem 6.1 literally writes liminf as J tends to infinity followed by an arrow to one as J tends to infinity. This redundant limiting syntax is preserved rather than changed to an equality or a single limit. The intended probability-one asymptotic assertion is explained separately.

The feasible initialization assumes a well-defined marginal MLE and exact local conditional draws. The source does not specify tie-breaking, measurable selection, a procedure for failed maximization, or a global computational guarantee for finding the MLE.

The uniform ball around the MLE is not explicitly intersected with a constrained hyperparameter domain. The model often uses R^D notation, while examples include positive precisions. Domain containment and valid conditional densities for every sampled point need attention when instantiating the source formula; no truncation is silently inserted.

The feasible-start section uses l in R^(lJ+D), whereas Section 4 uses ell for the local dimension. The symbols are recorded as printed, with their intended identification noted. The hierarchical dimension changes with J and is not placed directly in the fixed common-space setup of Section 2.

The exact two-block order updates local parameters first and hyperparameters second. The warm-start mixing theorem is not automatically a theorem for a different scan or for Metropolis-within-Gibbs approximations. The source discusses such extensions as future work.

value.description: Theorem 1 describes the conditional resampling law for general true and learned laws; it does not assume conditional independence or guarantee Type-I error control by itself. Theorem 2 explicitly restricts the true law to the null class.

Theoretical dCRT decisions use the infinite-resampling limit and a strict comparison to a conditional quantile. The finite-M algorithm has a plus-one corrected p-value and a non-strict resampled-tail comparison. The main Theorems do not quantify Monte Carlo error for a fixed number of resamples.

The fitted predictor kernel is learned from (X,Z) and the response mean from (Y,Z). Resampled predictors are independent across observations conditional on the original data, and nuisance estimates are held fixed. Original fitted residuals need not be unconditionally independent.

The same raw fitted-mean residual-product functional is used by GCM and dCRT. Evaluating GCM requires fitted means and an empirical variance, not a complete learned predictor kernel or resampling. The extra kernel-to-mean identity is retained with Algorithm 1, rather than imposed as an algorithmic prerequisite of the GCM optimality theorem.

The resampling variance (11) averages learned predictor variances times squared observed response residuals. The GCM variance (10) is the empirical variance of residual products. These are different finite-sample quantities; Theorem 2 asserts their ratio converges to one under its hypotheses.

The empirical variance notation in (10) does not explicitly select the n versus n-1 divisor or a zero-denominator decision rule. The census preserves the operator rather than inventing a finite-sample normalization. Asymptotic nondegeneracy does not by itself define the statistic on every exceptional dataset.

NDG2 is a comma-separated chain imposing strict positivity and finiteness on the learned predictor variance and both squared response residuals. NDG1 is a distinct probability lower bound on the total resampling variance. Theorem 2 names NDG2 but does not add NDG1 as an explicit premise.

Definition 1 requires conditional CDF convergence in probability at every continuity point of the limiting CDF. The conditioning sigma-field varies with n. The result is not recorded as almost-sure conditional convergence or merely unconditional asymptotic normality.

Lyap-1 uses observed fitted response residual powers; Lyap-2 instead uses conditional true response residual moments given Z_i. Both use learned predictor moments conditional on the full (X,Z) sample. They are not identical conditions and neither is replaced by a generic finite-moment assumption.

Lyap-1 explicitly quantifies some delta>0. Lyap-2 uses delta without a fresh quantifier in Theorem 2; SP2 already supplies a positive moment exponent. The source’s notation is retained, with a compatible positive exponent required to interpret the displayed condition.

The error quantities are empirical root-mean-square errors evaluated at the training covariates, including opposite-variable variance weights. The additional error in (24) uses a learned predictor-variance weight, unlike E-prime_n,y. No cross-fitting or independent training sample is assumed.

Variance consistency (23) is a signed weighted average of errors. It does not require absolute-error convergence or uniform pointwise variance estimation. The source’s weaker displayed condition is preserved.

SP1 is a product-rate requirement together with two weighted errors. SP1-prime adds the learned-variance-weighted response error. Theorem 3 requires SP1 and SP2, not the stronger SP1-prime used by Theorem 2.

Theorem 3 works at fixed p, whereas the earlier laws may form a triangular array with growing p. Its GPLM alternative model fixes the predictor/covariate law and uses a canonical exponential-family response. That model need not contain every null law in R.

Condition (36) has two alternative branches: constant positive second log-partition derivative with finite predictor second moment, or compact support of (X,Z) with continuous nuisance functions. The census preserves the OR and does not impose both branches simultaneously.

The nuisance space H_g is a linear subspace of L2, not explicitly a closed subspace. Condition (37) requires the conditional predictor mean itself to belong to H_g, not merely its closure. Function equivalence classes and continuous representatives need compatible choices when instantiating the compact-support branch.

The local-path definition (31) is stated for positive coefficient direction, but (38) evaluates the same formula at direction zero. The base g_0 dependence is suppressed in theta_n. The eventual sample-size threshold in (38) may depend on g_0 and h_g; no uniform threshold over the whole nuisance space is stated.

Definition 2 compares limsup competitor power with liminf power of the candidate test, first at a fixed direction, then for every direction and base nuisance function. LAUMP is not rewritten as a limit uniform over directions or nuisance functions.

The asymptotic level definition (4) takes the supremum over null laws before limsup in n. Theorem 3 condition (35) says SP1/SP2 hold for all laws in R, without explicit uniform versions in its wording. This quantifier distinction is retained; pointwise stochastic rates are not silently promoted to uniform rates.

Equation (34) defines s squared; the power formula uses s. Its nonnegative-root interpretation is recorded in the ambient resolution, without replacing the source formula. There is no source natural-language name for this scalar, so its original definition is retained with the local-path context rather than assigned an invented API title.

The GPLM source writes L_{beta,eta} in (29), while local parameters are pairs (beta,g). The natural predictor eta depends on X and Z, so the displayed product is a marginal law combined with a conditional response kernel, not independence of the response from covariates.

The source does not specify detailed measurable-selection conventions for learned conditional laws, fitted functions or conditional quantiles. The resampling formulas require suitable versions, and the ordinary probabilistic little-o notation is interpreted under the sequence of true data laws.

Proposition 4 skips item (iv) in its printed numbering. The auxiliary transcription preserves (i),(ii),(iii),(v),(vi),(vii) without inventing a missing item.
The wavelet basis paragraph uses 2^{j0}-1 in the displayed index range even for level j. Its detailed boundary construction is deferred to Appendix A; no corrected tensor index range is substituted.
The wavelet density formula equates an empirical sum over the entire Psi-bc basis with a truncated sum through J_n. The source inconsistency remains visible in the original passage.
The main text specifies N>=2 and j0>=log2(N), but does not spell out the needed wavelet regularity relative to an arbitrary alpha in Theorem 10. No Appendix A condition is guessed.

The normalized estimated densities are clipped at zero. The general estimated transport map is stated to be unique only almost everywhere under its estimated source law; the later population loss needs the source choice of a representative. No extra global uniqueness assertion is made.

Generic smooth-domain condition C1 replaces S1 unit-cube containment. Requiring both would incorrectly eliminate the intended generic-domain setting.

Theorem 20 ends with a comma after its final display. The following prose and footnote are discussion, not part of the theorem.

Shared gamma_1 and gamma_2 in the regression assumptions are minima of covariate and noise exponents. Their combined gamma uses a factor two absent from Theorem 4 gamma(Z).

The Lasso penalty is lambda times the square root of interval length times the L1 norm. Algorithm 1 divides the whole objective by interval length consistently with this scaling.
The source uses one zeta for both the partition penalty and the minimum interval length. Remark 1 distinguishes their roles but says the theory uses equal values.

The source interval loss omits the response-square sum and sets the loss to zero on short intervals. These printed choices are retained without asserting equivalence to another objective in every boundary case.

Lemma 2 states existence and finiteness of sigma_infty squared, but does not explicitly state strict positivity. Theorem 3 divides by sigma_infty; positive marginal noise variance alone is not substituted for an explicit positive directional long-run variance assumption.

Sections 4 and 4.1 explicitly discuss vanishing jumps. Theorems 8 and 10 refer back to Theorem 3, which has both regimes; the surrounding section restriction is retained separately rather than rewriting the theorem body.

Main text and references end on page 36. Numbered Section 5 is main text, while the actual attached supplement starts on page 37. Supplement mathematics is excluded.

Barred Sigma is the unconditional covariance; unbarred Sigma_t is the conditional covariance. Matrix/vector Latin symbols are bold upright. The iid reference is coupled through the same z_t, not a newly independent innovation sample.
The source defines the iid comparator for t=1,...,T but defines its sample covariance using t=1,...,n. The main-text passage does not identify T with n.
Assumption 1 requires a nonzero limiting population law and an upper spectral-norm bound. It does not impose positive definiteness of every population covariance or a positive lower eigenvalue bound.
The scalar eta uses sqrt(p(1-a-b)) inside a minimum with one. The coefficient denominator is 1-a-b, not its square root.
Theorem 2 asserts only a positive gap between expected empirical spectral second moments. The heavier-tail prose is not strengthened to a stochastic-order or Levy-distance theorem.
The QMLE is printed as argmax of the positive Gaussian contrast, without the usual negative sign. Preserve its optimization direction and objective literally.
The QMLE uses a randomly selected single coordinate. Remark 1 discusses pooling only as a practical alternative; a pooled estimator is not substituted into the theorem dependencies.

The QMLE parameter domain constrains the unconditional marginal variance by delta<=bar-sigma^2<C, while Assumption 1 allows singular population covariances. The main-text construction does not specify how the selected coordinate is guaranteed to satisfy that lower bound.

The main text does not specify the QMLE initialization, all candidate conditional variance recursions at finite sample boundaries, or a measurable tie-selection rule. The cited external algorithmic details remain unresolved.
The source calls P_t a projection matrix, but its formula is a weighted covariance matrix plus an identity term. Idempotence or orthogonality is not inferred from the name.

The projection uses M_p presample returns when t is small. The main-text definition does not detail how those observations or an initialization are supplied. M_p is an integer lag count with the displayed asymptotic growth.
The covariance estimators are uncentered outer-product averages divided by n. No estimated-mean subtraction or n-1 normalization is inserted.
Equation (2.9) uses y, while Theorem 4 equation (2.12) uses y^{-1} twice. Both source formulas are retained rather than reconciled by editing.
The generalized ESD (2.10) divides by tr(g(bar-Sigma)), but its generalized transform (2.11) divides by p. They are not silently treated as the same normalized transform.

For a merely bounded g, the generalized ESD denominator can be zero and the weights need not be nonnegative. The source does not add positivity or nonzero-trace hypotheses; equation (2.11) itself does not require this denominator.

Theorem 4 restricts g on the support interval of the limiting H but applies g to finite-dimensional population eigenvalues. It does not explicitly specify a global extension of g or require every such eigenvalue to lie in that interval.
Theorem 4 gives convergence for each z in the upper half-plane, without uniform-in-z or almost-sure quantification. Its limit is bound inline and is not separately inventoried as another Theorem.
The clipping threshold L is called a large constant without a quantitative lower bound here. Tau labels clipping, not a separate threshold value. Eigenvectors are preserved.

The Ledoit–Wolf (2015) nonlinear shrinkage algorithm is invoked by reference; its complete numerical construction is not in this main-text passage. The census records an unresolved external definition and does not substitute the oracle formula.

The oracle zero-eigenvalue branch uses the companion boundary value check-m_{underline F}(0) only when y>1. The printed otherwise branch also covers boundary cases not separately analyzed here, including zero eigenvalues with y=1.
The oracle nonzero branch uses an ordinary squared denominator without absolute-value bars. Complex boundary values can make this distinction substantive, so the source formula is not repaired.

Only the F subscript is underlined in the companion m_{underline F}. The source boundary-value definition writes check-m without an F subscript on the left, despite using indexed boundary values in (2.13).

The companion expression uses an indicator printed with braces around [0,infinity). This notation is preserved. Existence/nonvanishing of all boundary values used in the oracle is not separately stipulated in the main-text definition.

Theorem 5 inherits the assumptions of Theorem 4, including its g condition, but not its conclusion. Its metric is a dimension-normalized Frobenius difference from the oracle, not consistency to the unconditional covariance itself.

External results on QMLE rates, MP limits and oracle optimality are cited as justifications. They are not additional inventoried Theorems or proof-derived dependencies. QuEST population-spectrum consistency is Corollary 1 and is excluded from the Theorem inventory.

Main text and references end above y=137.4 on page 26; Appendix A begins at y=137.4128 on the same page. All appendix mathematics is excluded.
Theorem 5.1 spans pages 12–13 and includes the full remainder plus the optional initial-assignment extension. Omitting page 13 would change both the bound and the scope.

The Markov sufficient statistic uses blackboard-bold S; stage endpoints use plain S; the controlled state space uses script S. The initial inventory typography was corrected before the final census handoff.
Policy-dependent change time uses a subscript script X. Individual treatment X_t is italic, while the full assignment rule is script X. Sans-serif P,E,D and script U,R are preserved.
The observed filtration does not include the latent state. The response law nevertheless conditions on the latent current state and past latent history to specify conditional independence.

Assignment rules are deterministic and predictable, with a deterministic first treatment. The source mentions randomized policies as a possible extension, but the census does not enlarge the admissible class.
The initial hazard pi_0 and subsequent functions pi_t take values below one. The source permits a zero prior and zero hazards; it does not add a universal positive lower hazard bound.
The Markovian model requires only a fixed-dimensional sufficient treatment state. Finite memory is a separate example, not an assumption of Theorem 3.1 or of the other Theorems.

The posterior-odds definition may have a zero denominator under unrestricted response densities. The controlled state space is printed as R_+=[0,infinity), without an added infinite state or a separate likelihood-support condition in Theorem 3.1.
The controlled termination indicator is 1{t>T}, whereas the stopping action is 1{T=t}. Their one-step timing difference is preserved.

The predictive density phi used in transition formula (8) is explicitly defined in Appendix B.1, equation (B.1). Its formula remains unresolved under the main-text-only scope; no inferred mixture is inserted into the original source.
The source names link/update functions without an explicit global measurability or regularity condition in (1). Such hypotheses are not silently added to the Markov model.
The action-specific conditional expectation is written using conditioning on exact state values. The main-text display does not choose a version on null conditioning events.

The optimal policy uses argmin without an explicit measurable tie-selection rule. The stopping comparison is printed with the optimal total value J_c^*, and is not replaced by a different continuation value.

The auxiliary objective minimizes c times total sample size plus false-alarm probability. It does not minimize detection delay or enforce a prescribed false-alarm equality; the latter calibration is only discussed after Theorem 3.1.
The crossing time sigma allows zero additional observations, while tau starts at one. Displayed inequalities are non-strict even where surrounding prose says exceeds or smaller than.
The proposed procedure restarts block indexing and the likelihood-ratio test at each stage. It terminates in favor of detection when the two crossing times tie.
The initial deterministic prefix in (11) applies only in the first acceleration stage and may be cut short at S_1. It is not repeated in every cycle.

The source states stopping constructions via infima without a comprehensive rule for infinite stage endpoints or all zero-duration boundary cases. The formulas are retained without inventing such conventions.

Condition (14) explicitly puts a positive lower bound on V_x^I, and only a finite upper bound on V_x^J. Both are centered log-likelihood second moments, although the block-averaging prose calls them second moments.

The uniform stability condition (16) quantifies over every starting time, prior treatment history and cyclic phase. M(Xi,epsilon) is a sufficient positive integer, not specified as the smallest possible threshold.
The adjusted information D(Xi)=I(Xi)+d(Xi) uses sans-serif D. The threshold d in the switching rule is unrelated to the block log-hazard limit d(Xi).

Theorem 5.1 is non-asymptotic and holds for arbitrary stated thresholds and blocks under its conditions. The optimized threshold formulas, later dominance convention D(Xi_2)>=D(Xi_1), and finite-memory block designs are not extra assumptions.

The initial expected-time formula lambda(Xi) includes 1-pi_0. The worst-history residual formula tilde-lambda omits it; the accompanying prose does not explicitly state conditioning on no previous change, so that interpretive detail is kept outside the original quotation.

The uniform two-block hazard bound zeta may be zero and the worst-history expected time may be infinite. Theorem 5.1 does not separately assert their positivity or finiteness, so its displayed bound can be uninformative in such cases.
Theorem 6.1 uses an alpha-indexed change model with fixed response densities. The asymptotic bound is defined through a liminf ratio, not an additive remainder or a finite-alpha inequality.
Condition (27) is uniform over time and all treatment histories, not only the two selected blocks. Its displayed t>=0 includes the prior pi_0 despite the different notation used for it in the setup.
Condition (28) requires existence of a block controlling the worst-history residual duration. It does not restrict all assignment rules in the universal lower bound to that block.

Condition (29) assumes D-star>0 and D-star=O(1), without stating a lower bound away from zero. It writes epsilon>0, although its window floor((1-epsilon)|log(alpha)|/D-star) is nonpositive for epsilon>=1; no corrected range is substituted.

The information-bound expression in (29) repeats the policy quantifier before a supremum over policies, and its summands can involve random treatment histories. A pathwise or probability interpretation of that supremum is not additionally specified in the displayed assumption.

The universal lower bound does not inherit uniform block-stability (16), the cyclic procedure, optimized blocks or the Markovian restriction. Omega is reused as a scalar definition without importing its surrounding stability hypothesis.

The density phi is the only appendix-only formula needed by the stored construction. Appendix proofs, exponential/polynomial-decay examples, posterior formulas for unknown parameters and simulation details are not used to complete these three theorem statements.

Sigma imposes local Lipschitz regularity, global linear growth and inward drift outside [-A,A]. Its C>=1 parameter convention is not explicitly reconciled with C/2-eta in later tightened reference classes.

The invariant density has a normalized exponential signed integral from zero to x. The density can be used as a deterministic weight without assuming the observed process starts in that invariant law.

Sections 2–5 use stationary P_b and E_b. Section 6 fixes x0 and a common unsubscripted P,E; those laws must not be conflated. Remark 5.5 points to supplement-only details for fixed-point extensions of the earlier results.
The simple null is equality on [-A,A]. References to the simple hypothesis {b0} do not justify changing it into equality of drifts everywhere on R.
K_y,h has no 1/h amplitude prefactor. The rational index set includes only pairs whose location interval lies inside [-A,A].

Theorem 3.1 allows signed continuous bounded-variation kernels of norm at most one. Theorem 4.1 additionally requires nonnegativity. Theorem 5.2 uses norm exactly one and does not restate continuity. Section 6 adds C1 to the conditions of Theorem 4.1.

The local score has an explicit zero-denominator value zero; Lambda has a zero-over-zero rule, and Upsilon has a zero-over-zero convention for its argument. The empirical maximum scale retains the squared indicator from the source.

Upsilon at zero is given by a printed logarithm-times-indicator expression. Its intended convention must not be replaced by ordinary arithmetic on an undefined logarithm. Gaussian ratio formulas may also degenerate when K=0, permitted by the printed <=1 condition.
U1 and U2 are driven by the same W in the source; no independence is stated. Both normalizers use Lebesgue L2 and the appropriate boundary-drift density.
Finite-T null quantiles and the limiting similarity threshold are distinct. Both use minimum and a non-strict CDF inequality, while both tests reject with a strict inequality.

Delta_J depends on the alternative density q_b. Its infimum-of-norms definition is nonnegative, but the following supremum formula omits a positive part and can be negative when band violation occurs only outside J. Both formulas are preserved.

The Holder lower integer is strictly smaller than beta, even at integer beta. The printed condition quantifies over k but displays only a derivative of order floor(beta); no derivative sup-norm constraints are inserted.
The separation rate delta_T and sharp constant c_* are distinct from the arbitrary sufficient c(beta,L,K) and the later Hurst neighborhood delta(T,epsilon). The star in c_* is a subscript.

The explicit optimal recovery kernel formula is stated for beta<=1 only. General beta has compact support but not a main-text guarantee that this support is exactly [-1,1], raising a normalization issue for its use in the earlier fixed-support statistic.
Theorem 5.3 prints (b,L) in its outer infimum over the beta,L rectangle. The source index mismatch is retained, not corrected to (beta,L).
Theorem 5.3 does not explicitly restate the K=K_beta choice in its sharp-L assertion. Its context from Theorem 5.2 is recorded without inventing a new explicit hypothesis.

Theorem 5.4 follows an eta=0 paragraph but refers to b0 and epsilon_T from Theorem 5.2. Its power-one condition prints (1-epsilon_T)c_*delta_T; the minus sign is retained as an apparent conflict with the matching lower-bound interpretation.
The pathwise integral functional suppresses its y,h dependence in the symbol tilde-I_T. Its formula uses classical integrals and the fixed sigma^2/2 correction.
D_A,T requires a path to visit both -A and A. The source claim that this prevents zero denominators does not cover the zero kernel permitted by its inherited kernel condition.
The pathwise statistic defines a function of f but still prints X in its Lambda term. The original formula and the surrounding ordinary-integral explanation are preserved separately.
The exact h_min(T) threshold is deferred to Remark B.1 in Appendix B. The main-text restricted index set is saved, with that missing formula explicitly unresolved.
Fractional Brownian covariance does not determine the cross-H coupling. The common Volterra representation is given, but K_H is specified only in Appendix I equation (I.8), which is excluded.
Theorem 6.3 contains a conditional probability statement and both orders of iterated liminf for the conditioning event. They are not collapsed to a single unconditional limit.

Theorem 6.5 does not rebind epsilon_T,beta,L,J in its body; the preceding lower-bound reference supplies context but not a rewritten statement. Its displayed hypothesis classes do not repeat the global-Lipschitz restriction used to introduce the coupled solution notation.

Theorem 6.5 concerns all uniformly level tests and preserves the supremum over H followed by the supremum over tests and infimum over alternatives. The proposed pathwise test in Remark 6.4 is not imposed on that all-test class.

Theorem 4 literally requires b/n+n/b^2→infinity while importing assumptions of Theorem 3, which require the same expression to approach zero. The contradiction is explicitly retained and not repaired.
Theorem 4 gives u as the Jacobian rank at theta0 and assumes C1 near theta0, without explicitly requiring a constant rank in a neighborhood. No stronger rank condition is added to the original claim.

Pinned arXiv:2305.11672v2, 73 pages, dated 2 May 2024. Main text PDF1–22 ends in funding; Sections S1–S5 starting on PDF23 and following references are excluded. Exact final-journal equivalence is not asserted.
Two actual main-text Theorems are preserved in full. Main-text Propositions 3–6 and supplementary Lemmas/Propositions/Theorems are not added to the Theorem inventory.

Training triples are iid; only masked features, full labels and masks are observed. The test point is fully observed and has the unconditional marginal P_Q, not the conditional complete-case distribution.
The theorem expectations condition on every training mask. Positive probability is required for each specified o in O; the source does not require Q to put zero mask mass outside O.
Masking leaves vectors in R^d with zero-filled coordinates. The mask distinguishes an observed zero from an unobserved coordinate. Lower-density dimension d_omega may differ from this ambient d.

The original missingness assumption equates subvector regression probabilities at all support points and all compatible masks. It allows dependence and examples of missing not at random; it is not replaced by an MCAR assumption.

Pointwise conditional probabilities and conditional expectations are used outside an almost-everywhere formulation. The source does not explicitly fix versions everywhere on support; no version regularity is added.

The anova recursion subtracts all strict-predecessor components inside the conditional expectation, with a centered constant component. The source describes these functions as orthogonal without imposing independent feature coordinates in the general setup. The recursion and description are retained without certifying that assertion or substituting a different decomposition.
The signal sigma_omega^2 is a conditional second moment minimized over compatible masks, not a centered variance. It may be zero in the minimax theorem because c_E=0 is allowed; HAM requires c_E>0.
Minima over compatible masks occur in the signal and tail definitions even for patterns not contained in any o in O. No explicit empty-minimum convention is given in the inspected main text.

U(Omega) is the complement of Omega and its strict lower closure, so it includes incomparable patterns. It is not only the strict upper closure. The displayed braces around the removed union are preserved as printed grouping.

The unconditional masked measure mu_omega and conditional training measure mu_{omega|o} remain distinct. Definition 3 evaluates conditional lower-density events under the unconditional test measure; Definition 3+ additionally uses every conditional measure on the outside.
Lower density uses open balls and radii 0<r<1; its exponent can be less than ambient dimension. It does not require an ordinary density or a uniform positive bound.
The margin event is |eta-1/2|<t and includes exact ties; no additional 0<|eta-1/2| restriction is inserted. Bayes and HAM both choose class one at a tie.
Counts n_omega are the number of containing realized masks, not exact-pattern counts or expected counts. Script N and prescribed script O have different meanings.

Theorem 1 allows Omega_star intersect N to be empty. Then the printed definition of R and the minimum inside its logarithm have empty domains, with no explicit convention in the main text. The unavailable-pattern indicator communicates the intended constant-risk regime but does not define those empty extrema.

Theorem 1 retains its exact lower-bound-only margin and constant restrictions. Its upper bound adds the unavailable-pattern indicator outside the C times logarithmic rate product. The constants may depend on class parameters but not n or the realized mask sequence.

Theorem 2 uses C_L>=1 while the introductory domain for Q-prime-Miss in (11) states C_L>1. Definition 3 and Definition 3+ allow C_L>=1; the plus-class replacement implicitly extends that introductory domain, without changing the original text.

Algorithm 1 uses k_omega=1+floor(n_omega^a) without capping at n_omega. At n_omega=1 this requests two neighbors from one available case. Theorem 2 does not impose a lower sample size on active and lower patterns. Main-text Section 5.2 separately writes k_omega in [n_omega] for its proof quantities but does not change Algorithm 1 or supply a cap.

Algorithm 1 admits zero coordinate tail parameters. For processed patterns with gamma_omega=0 and alpha=0, its tuning exponents have zero numerator and denominator. Positivity on active patterns alone does not explicitly cover coordinates outside their union.

Algorithm 1 line 7 calls projected feature/label pairs a reordering of pairs retaining the original masks o_i. The first last-neighbor X subscript also omits the pattern index that appears in the corresponding distance expression. Both printed forms are preserved.

Algorithm 1 loops over evaluations at X_i^{o_i} and x0, but line 10 evaluates fitted components at X_i^omega. Its intended dependence only on x^omega makes those compatible conceptually; the printed finite evaluation loop does not explicitly implement that extension.

Algorithm 1 line 15 requires U({omega}) intersect hat-Omega to be empty. Because U includes incomparable patterns, this condition can suppress incomparable candidates after one is selected, unlike the prose that says only predecessors are disregarded. No corrected set condition is substituted.

Nearest-neighbor distance ties and the traversal order of equal-dimensional patterns are unspecified. Combined with the printed selection condition, different within-level orders can select different surviving incomparable patterns.

Algorithm 1 line 2 writes a bold zero subscript without d; this is retained rather than silently changing it to the population notation f_{0_d}. The reconstruction excludes the constant term if hat-Omega is empty, as printed.

Theorem 2 sample-size condition uses an ordinary logarithm with the full exponent 4[gamma_omega(2 beta_omega+d_omega)+alpha beta_omega]/(beta_omega gamma_omega). Its conclusion uses log-plus=log(max(x,e)), not log(1+x).

The HAM procedure is stored as one complete algorithmic definition; its inline temporary quantities are not split into invented population interfaces. The oracle algorithm, Assouad lemma and proof concentration events are not imported into statement dependencies.

The pinned source is the 26-page final published PDF. Page 23 describes an external supplement; it is not the beginning of an appendix body inside this PDF. References end on page 26. The supplement was not opened.

All six actual main-text Theorems are preserved. Lemmas, Corollaries, Remarks and citations are not additional theorem records. Corollary 4.5 contributes hypotheses because Theorem 4.6 explicitly invokes them.

Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 4.6 both contain substantial material after their initial conclusions. All of that italic material is included; in particular Theorem 4.6 includes the total-risk and expected-distance bounds.
The unnumbered Assumption prints the conditioning index y in Omega although the conditional kernel domain uses Omega_Y. This source notation is retained.

The central class consists of all square-integrable central-field-measurable functions and can be infinite dimensional. It is not the span of the d generating coordinates and is not inherently mean-zero.

Remark 3.3 declares all functions mean-zero. The later class of neural networks with biases is not explicitly centered. Since centered losses and variance penalties are translation invariant, proportionality up to sign in Theorem 3.7 and distance to plus/minus a function require attention to that convention; no centering operation is inserted into the source estimator.

GMDD uses a Levy measure and a cndf-induced difference kernel. Full integrability, symmetry and support conditions sufficient for the displayed equivalence and zero-characterization are not provided here. The main text points to external references [4,35]. No unverified extra conditions are presented as original assumptions.
The Levy measure mu in Section 2.2 and the later scalar/vector optimization penalties reuse the same letter with different meanings. Tilde-mu is a separate cross-direction penalty.

Theorem 3.2 assumes an optimizer exists. Its upper bound m<=dimension of the full central class does not independently ensure enough nonconstant normalized directions. The theorem is not rewritten as an existence assertion.
Assumption A1 requires distinct first d+1 ordered negative GMDD values, not just the first d. It also constrains tilde-mu. Theorem 3.8 does not state A1.
The Frobenius penalty is unsquared; the successive variance and covariance penalties are squared. Theorem 3.8 is a population claim and does not refer to the separate empirical implementation.

The sample passage defines D_n from observed pairs but does not explicitly write an iid assumption there. The U-statistic analysis uses independent observations in its prose; the exact general sampling assumption and measurable argmin selections need specification in formalization.

The order-four empirical objectives require a meaningful inverse binomial(n,4), ordinarily n>=4. Theorem 4.2 states n>=V and has an n-3 denominator, while Theorem 4.4 does not explicitly restate either restriction. No extra restriction is inserted into the original bodies.

I_{n,k} contains all ordered distinct-index tuples; J_{n,k} contains only increasing tuples. The kernels use I_{4,k}, while the U-statistic average uses J_{n,4}. All printed coefficients are retained.

The empirical recursion uses previous estimated directions; the excess risk fixes previous population directions. The first-direction estimator uses no covariance kernel, so Theorems 4.2 and 4.4 do not inherit the later-step kernel merely because it occurs nearby.

A2 bounds all candidate functions and the kernel at every pair of response-space points. Its prose says bounded Y can ensure boundedness, but that does not literally bound a kernel on all R^q. A2 also requires a uniform bound on a candidate class otherwise described by architecture alone.

The Holder definition is restricted to beta in (0,1] and a function-dependent existential zeta on the unit cube. No common Holder radius, derivative-based extension or explicit support reduction of the general X law is supplied in that definition.

A4 does not specify the range of epsilon. Its right-hand side becomes negative for sufficiently large epsilon, so an unrestricted all-positive-epsilon reading is not silently imposed. V depends on the candidate class and may therefore depend on n.

The sign-invariant rho is a pseudodistance on the unquotiented function space. C1 is only specified as an appropriate positive constant satisfying (12); its detailed choice is delegated to the excluded proof of Theorem 4.4.

Theorem 4.6 retains probability 1-(4j-3)delta for each j and then a summed bound. It does not separately state the simultaneous event probability for that sum; do not silently add a union bound or uniformity in d.

The last Theorem 4.6 clause invokes a ReLU class with a stated sample-dependent depth that is not rounded to an integer. The width parameter N is arbitrary, and the sample-size condition uses the resulting S and L. The generic positive-constant convention asserts independence of n, not independence of every architecture parameter.

Section 4.2 contains proof-level notational inconsistencies: R1,n is written with an extra argument in one L1,n term and the displayed first-order sum omits the 1/n that appears in v1,n. These formulas are not theorem targets and are not substituted into the empirical estimator or rho definition.

Selection of tuning constants and the empirical Frobenius estimator are delegated to the supplement; the dimension-selection algorithm, simulation optimizer Adam and numerical examples are downstream uses, not hypotheses of these six Theorems.

Main-text references finish above the Appendix A heading on page 56. Appendix bodies and their theorem statements are excluded. Four actual main-text Theorems are 2,3,4,11; numbering gaps are other result types.

Experiments in Sections 2 and 3 have the same observable grid but different volatility laws and parameter domains. The general-model H<3/4 restriction is not replaced with the broader extension discussed in Section 4.
The source normalizes sigma_0^2=1 in Section 2 and sigma_0=1 in Section 3. Driver independence rules out a leverage effect; the companion paper is outside scope.

The minimax criterion is a liminf of infimum over all data-measurable estimators followed by supremum over parameters. It is not a pointwise lower bound or an expected-loss definition. Rate dependence on H is preserved.
Delta appears as delta_n in the block observations and as delta in the model and rates. The source permits a sequence but does not separately spell out every limiting regime in the theorem bodies.

Page 5 defines n=2^N and m=n delta integer. Page 7 indexes block observations below delta_n^-1, but its empirical coefficient indices use 2^(N-j). Their compatibility for arbitrary m is unresolved; no automatic redefinition of N is made.

The coarse estimator on page 8 uses log, whereas the general estimator uses log_2. The coarse original is preserved; its intended logarithm base and the claimed consistency need clarification rather than silent correction.
Equation (5), not needed to evaluate the retained coarse estimator, contains an extra 2^-j in its middle noise subscript. It is not used to repair or redefine the empirical coefficient formula.

Coarse scale selection explicitly ranges from 2 to N-1 and returns 2 on an empty set. The general selections omit both the range and the empty-set fallback; these are not transferred without evidence.

Both constructions can encounter nonpositive noise-corrected energy estimates. The source does not fully define off-event logarithm, ratio, square-root and empty-maximum conventions. Clamping the eventual value does not itself define these intermediate operations.

The general latent definition states k<2^p but its Q sum uses k<2^(j-1). General empirical expressions also permute j,p,k in d and e, and the estimated Q sum leaves the k range implicit. Exact originals and auxiliary target context are retained.
The noise correction is 6 Var(bar epsilon_m)2^(-j-p) in the coarse model versus 2^(-j-p+1) Var(log xi^2) in the general model. Hat d^2 denotes an estimate of a square, not a squared estimate.

The initial general estimates are projected to the bounding rectangle, which need not equal the compact D. The scale hat j_n depends on the initial H estimate and remains fixed in later eta corrections.

The iteration is sequential: the mth eta update uses H^(m) and eta^(m-1), not H^(m-1). The theorem retains the extra intermediate m in m_opt>m>1/(4H)-2H-1, although the preceding construction only states the weaker m_opt inequality.
The truncation S is an integer constrained by both S>=1/(4H_-)+1/2 and S>H_+/(2H_-)-1/2. It is not the price process S_t, and it is distinct from iteration m and block length m reused elsewhere.

The Gaussian-integral definition uses an uncentered W for total degree b=1 and increments for b>=2. Factorials and the distinction between plain fractional Brownian W and fraktur integral W are preserved.

The overlined sum on page 31 restricts multi-index entries to {1,...,S}, whereas the preceding W and g definitions use {1,...,2S}. Equation (36) retains the stated overlined-sum convention; its truncation dependence is not simplified.

Kappa_{p,a} is available in main-text equation (36), even though it is inside a proof section. Its W-integral and index definitions are included because the estimator consumes them. Isserlis expansion, remainder Z, H-star and surrounding proof lemmas are not extra statement dependencies.

The bias function has argument order (I,nu), with sum starting at a=2. Lemma 10 later reverses parameter names in its displayed arguments; this proof-bound formula is not used to change the estimator definition.

Theorem 11 is boundedness in probability uniformly over D, not a central limit theorem or moment-risk bound. Theorem 3 similarly asserts uniform tightness, without distributional or expected-error conclusions.

Appendix C supplies a trigamma expression and moment bound for the coarse noise, but the noise distribution itself is defined in the main text. The census uses that distribution to resolve its variance and does not import an appendix formula.

For i>=1 each known operator has exactly one nonzero coefficient type, of order 0,1 or 2. The nuisance A0 can mix orders. Formal adjoints reverse the constant transport sign.

The main setup allows an F0-measurable X0, but later describes all generalized observations as Gaussian. Gaussianity does not follow from arbitrary F0-measurability alone. The original descriptions are retained; the lower-bound model separately imposes stationarity.

The source describes cylindrical solutions as taking values in L2 subset H1 or H subset H1 while motivating a larger space because of roughness. Actual membership in the smaller space is not silently assumed in the census; the generalized pairing is retained.

Observation kernels are L2-scaled by delta^(-d/2). Observations are entire time paths. Disjoint supports imply independent driving Brownian motions, not independent observed processes; the source explicitly warns about this distinction.

The augmented MLE comes from a modified likelihood after ignoring certain dependencies and initial information. The explicit estimator, including its A0 correction, is retained rather than identifying it with an exact independent-diffusion MLE.
The Fisher information convention has no kernel-variance divisor. The Gaussian covariance in both CLT forms includes norm(K)^2. Neither K normalization nor an extra noise-scale factor is inserted.
H(ii) is strict: n_i>1-d/2. The boundary-case extensions in Section 5 and Proposition 5.3 do not modify the inventoried Theorem 2.3.

H(iii) requires a compact interior location set independent of both delta and M and eventual disjointness. L(iii) instead requires strict delta separation and disjoint supports for the fixed configuration, without the same interior compact-set condition.
H(iv) is a uniform little-o bound on the propagated initial signal. The stationary-law requirement in L is different and is not replaced by H(iv) or by the sufficient examples of Lemma 2.2.

The whole-space positive principal operator is assigned the multiplier (-xi^T a_theta xi)^s in the source. This conflicts with its positivity and the usual sign convention; the exact original is retained separately from this note.
The RKHS norm for the stationary convolution includes fractional endpoint penalties at both 0 and T. These are not zero-boundary constraints in time.

Theorem 3.2 binds arbitrary kernels in D(A), not just spatially localized kernels. It requires nonsingular Gram G and its bound has squared inverse-Gram norm times norm(G_A), plus a distinct inverse-Gram term and derivative contribution.

The covariance-based RKHS definition (6.8) sums over strictly positive eigenvalues of an orthonormal system. If the covariance has a nontrivial kernel, the printed finite-norm set needs a support/orthogonality convention to agree with the alternative range C_Z^(1/2)Z. No repair is inserted into the source passage.

Equation (6.7) in the main proof section integrates exp(-2 lambda_j t-prime) from minus infinity with an unshifted semigroup argument, making the displayed finiteness condition problematic. This proof construction is not imported as a definition or hypothesis of the retained RKHS statements.

The lower bounds use one-sided one-dimensional submodels through (1,0,0), with local neighborhoods that differ between the small-error and constant-error regimes. They are not unrestricted parameter-space lower bounds.

Theorem 4.3 inherits all of Theorem 4.1 and adds both derivative observation channels, three-kernel linear independence and all three instantiations of Assumption L. No appendix Corollary A.4 is required to state this extension.

Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 quantify constants depending only on K and an absolute c3, while requiring T>=1 and M>=1. The Gaussian theorem and CLT are different claims and no asymptotic normality or expected-risk conclusion is added to the lower bounds.

Nonzero kernel norms, meaningful inverse information, stochastic-integral measurability and unbounded-operator domains are consumed where the source supplies them through assumptions or contextual definitions; unspecified conventions are not silently converted into new original assumptions.

Seven original Theorems occur in main text. Theorem 2 continues on page 8 and Theorem 4 on page 11. Main text and references end above Appendix A on page 22; no appendix body is admitted.

The baseline consists of iid raw observations. Theorems 3-4 instead use retained stationary observations with gaps; Theorem 5 uses cycle reward-duration pairs. Reuse of the statistic formulas does not import iid raw observations into those settings.
The source defines the target as psi=psi(P), then prints psi_0 in W_SJ. The original target alias is preserved and explained rather than replaced in the formula.
The sample variance for batching centers at the average batch estimate; sectioning centers at the full empirical estimate. Their denominators and the SB hybrid are not interchangeable.
The sample variance formulas require K>1 and may vanish on finite samples. The source gives no totalized statistic value on a zero denominator; no convention is fabricated.
Theorem 1 assumes a uniform scalar Edgeworth expansion with alternating parity. The p_j here are not automatically the same objects as the density-weighted p_1,p_2 later defined for Algorithm 1.
Theorem 2 has separate K>=r+3 and K>=4 conclusions. The source comment about potentially relaxing K with a Peano remainder is not inserted into the original theorem.
Definition 1 uses sigma instead of alpha in its final alpha(n) expression. The two-field mixing formula is otherwise explicit. Both printed symbols are retained.
Definition 2 says there exists a measure mu, without nonzero or sigma-finite qualifications. These normally relevant requirements are not silently added to the quotation.
Theorem 3 prints the mixing limit as n->0, despite the surrounding large-batch-size setting. It is retained as printed.

Theorem 3 uses r derivatives of f whereas Theorem 2 uses r+1. Its uniform Cramer expression involves iuX_1 with vector u; the pairing convention and the role of g are not clarified by silently rewriting it.
Theorem 3 requires a recurrent atom but does not define one in the main text. It makes no symmetric-coverage O(n^-1) claim, as the following paragraph explicitly confirms.

Theorem 4 states only positive lambda while its split transition and residual kernel require probability-kernel constraints, including a meaningful inverse of 1-lambda. The binary-state range for delta is implicit, and delta is also used for the gap exponent.
Theorem 4 uses alpha for an initial distribution as well as alpha(n) for mixing, and P for both stationary law and transition kernel. The local roles are preserved and disambiguated in analysis.

Theorem 4 does not explicitly repeat a differentiability requirement on f. The general Section 5 regularity discussion is recorded without choosing and inserting an unstated derivative order into the theorem.
Theorem 4 uses G as a centered cycle sum, while Theorem 3 uses G as an absolute reward sum. The different definitions and starting laws in the moment conditions remain separate.

The regenerative construction starts at T_1 and excludes the initial incomplete cycle. Its target is a ratio of expectations, not an expectation of cycle ratios. No fixed calendar-time gap scheme is imposed on these pairs.
Theorem 6 inherits Theorem 2 with r=2 and targets the symmetric n^(-1) coefficient. Main-text discussion corroborates K>=5; the separate batching-only algorithm in Appendix C is excluded.
Algorithm 1 reuses X_i for freshly simulated Gaussian draws after taking original-law covariance and cumulants as inputs. This simulation step is not a Gaussian original-data assumption.

Equation (7) calls p_1,p_2 polynomials but includes the Gaussian density factor, and p_1 includes a leading 1. These exact source expressions are retained, not replaced by conventional Edgeworth density polynomials.

Algorithm 1 Step 3 divides a term in F_xx by an unexplained c. F_+ and F_- contain no division by the first gradient coordinate, although the stated hypotheses only require a nonzero gradient, not a normalized first coordinate.
Algorithm 1 Step 4 uses y_x, rather than y_x^(-), in the printed y_xx^(-) formula. It is not silently corrected.

Algorithm 1 Step 5 has no printed plus sign between the first bracketed term and the following parenthesis. It also uses p_1(x(A)) without specifying a scalar-versus-joint convention and has phi-prime only in the last negative-side term. All these expressions remain as printed.

The sectioning example alternates A_i and X_i and uses m and f_0 without a local definition. It prints b_2 as a contraction of the second-derivative tensor v with three vectors. No correction to w is inserted.

The sectioning prose names coefficients d,d-prime but its formulas and Algorithm 1 use lambda,lambda-prime. The inline factor 2 in the lambda-prime display is multiplication, not a superscript square; visual comparison resolved that typography.

Explicit Taylor coefficients for batching, SB and SJ are relegated to excluded Section B. The generic Taylor instructions in Algorithm 1 are preserved, but unavailable original formulas are not reconstructed and presented as quotations.

Theorem 7 fixes n and lets K grow, and gives no SB limit. Its spelling differantiable is retained. The source defines no full influence-function formula or tangent topology for its Gateaux assumption.
Theorem 7 places division by sigma outside the square root in both sectioning CDF arguments. A high-resolution crop confirms this; it is not a source error to be repaired.

The registered 49-page source is arXiv:2301.02168v2. The arXiv stamp is dated 7 January 2024 and the title page 9 January 2024; both are preserved. The filename and export URL in the register refer to the same pinned bytes.

Main text ends after Acknowledgments on page 22, before the appendix notation prelude at y=297.2278137207031. That prelude and all appendix bodies are excluded. Theorem 4.1 is within main text and is included despite appearing in a proof section.

The Gaussian approximation is redefined in Section 2 as the canonical solution of the first order equations in R_V. Global KL minimization is not required by these theorem statements; (1.1) is retained only as historical context.

Assumption 1 and the displayed growth conditions use a superscript star m^*, whereas the region and Lemma 2.1 use m_*; their source role is the same unique minimizer. The quotes keep their printed forms.

Assumption 2 prints q,a3,a4>0. The logistic specialization explicitly uses q=0 in Section 3.2 and Corollary 3.1. This boundary-value inconsistency is retained rather than changing the assumption to q>=0.

The weighted tensor supremum in (1.11) has no absolute value. For even tensor order this is not generally the usual norm. Preserve the formula and its stated equality to the multi-vector expression; do not silently insert absolute values or certify the cited assertion.

The region uses the norm of H_V^(1/2) S^(1/2), which need not be a symmetric matrix. The paper also uses standard matrix operator norms; do not restrict that product to the symmetric-tensor domain of (1.11).

Condition (2.7) involves the centered expectation and controls only the exterior of an ellipsoid. No explicit local measurability or integrability condition is stated there. Treat ordinary existence of expectations and variance as analytic well-formedness requirements rather than silently adding hypotheses to the original theorem.

The constants a3,a4,q,c0 and the potential v may depend on n and d in the general results. The suppressed constants have the dependencies named in each theorem; no unmentioned uniform asymptotic regime is inserted.

Theorem 3.1 inherits the logistic model, Gaussian design, bounded true coefficient and bounded prior precision from the paragraph immediately before it. Those assumptions are not present in the four-line opening alone and must remain attached to the theorem.

The final display for labels in Section 3 omits a conditioning bar, but preceding prose and (3.1) define the conditional Bernoulli law. The quoted display is not edited to add conditioning. The joint iid sampling interpretation is corroborated in Lemma 3.2.

Exactly Theorems 1, 2 and 4 occur in main text. Number 3 belongs to a Corollary. References end on page 23 and Appendix A begins separately on page 24; no appendix body was read.

Theorem 1 requires equality between a full-data KL infimum and an attained reduced-data minimum. It does not assert existence of a full-data minimizing pair, and V_n is any measurable statistic rather than a required invariant.
Theorem 1 has two potentially different probability priors on G. The optimum is a ratio of mixtures of reduced densities, not a mixture of likelihood ratios or an assumed Haar-prior Bayes factor.

Theorem 2 requires all three parts of Assumption 1 and amenability. Both log likelihood ratios have 1+epsilon moments, one under Q_1 and one under Q^{M_n}; the identity subscript is not a sample index.
Theorem 4 invokes only Part 3 of Assumption 1. For every g it requires some h with finite KL(Q_g,P_h); it does not require a single h to work for all g or finiteness for every pair.

Theorem 4 proves a constant oracle value and then equivalence of the sets of optimizers for the absolute and relative criteria. These definitions remain separate, and existence of an optimizer is not added to the theorem.

The source defines e-statistics as nonnegative real statistics, allowing zero. Logarithmic objectives therefore need the usual extended-value convention at zero; this and expectation well-definedness are not explicitly spelled out in the displayed definition.

The KL definition uses the Radon-Nikodym derivative dQ/dP but does not explicitly define the non-absolutely-continuous case. Finite KL requirements and common-support statements are preserved without fabricating a complete source convention.

Theorem 1 uses reduced densities without a separately printed dominating-measure specification in that theorem. Density existence and measurability are part of interpreting its formula; no extra Assumption 1 clauses are inserted into it.

Assumption 1 Part 1 says Polish followed by a dash and separable, completely metrizable and locally compact. All listed properties are retained; the wording is not taken to make local compactness part of the standard definition of Polish.

The main-text description of a topological group specifies continuity of the group operation but does not explicitly mention continuity of inversion. Preserve the description; a formalization must resolve this usual ambient convention.

Part 3 requires a common relatively left-invariant dominating measure and a single common support for all densities. It is not silently replaced by the left-invariant measure used in the subsequent proof.

The amenability definition on page 5 is a sequence with convergence separately for each measurable B and each g. No supremum over sets or uniform convergence on compact sets is written there; the source quantifiers are preserved.

Page 18 gives a second amenability formulation using increasing symmetric compact sets and a right-Haar ratio. The source calls it equivalent; this is retained as auxiliary context, without certifying equivalence or filling in unspecified positivity and empty-set conventions.
The componentwise action notation on page 4 switches from input x^n to capital gX^n. This typographical mismatch remains in the original passage.

Section 2.1 introduces independent copies and overloads P,Q between one-observation and sample laws. Pi^g is a mixture binding the group index; it is not group exponentiation. Q^{M_n} is instead an image law.

The reduced laws do not carry a group subscript because invariance removes that nuisance index within each of the two fixed invariant-parameter hypotheses. This does not identify null and alternative reduced laws with each other.

The reparameterization discussion uses free action on the parameter space to identify each orbit with G. The extracted testing problem is the resulting group-indexed model; no reparameterization proof or extra free-action clause is appended to Theorem 4.

Anytime-validity, martingales, optional stopping, composite-invariant-parameter extensions and example-specific formulas occur as propositions, corollaries or discussion. They are not additional Theorems and do not become dependencies of these three statements solely because they occur in the same paper.

The census checks original statements, source meanings and dependency paths. It does not certify the proofs or the paper's external group-theoretic equivalence claims, and it does not audit mathlib availability.

value: The inspected source is the registered 59-page arXiv:2308.04916v3 PDF, 29 May 2024. Main text ends after Funding on page 26, before the Supplementary Material heading; the supplement introduction and appendix bodies are excluded.

Exactly ten actual main-text Theorem environments occur, numbered 1-10. Theorem 6 and Theorem 7 each retain their two complete bullets in a single claim. The later application and remarks are not additional Theorems.

Generic constructions (3) and (4) share one original source passage but retain distinct single-index and wavelet branches. Basis coefficients are ambient objects usable without a prior, so smoothness balls and observation models do not depend on the prior construction.

Scale alternatives (5), (6) and (21) retain their original natural-language keyword and source labels. Identical keywords do not establish equivalent scales. Branch resolution specifies which scale, coefficient indexing and rate each theorem selects.

Conditions (7) and (8) constrain the innovation density. The logarithmic upper bound on 1/h is a lower bound on density decay, not an upper-tail condition. The constants c1>0 and kappa>=0 remain unchanged.

Moment condition (14) and tail condition (19) are different. An x^-2 survival bound need not give a finite second moment. Theorems 1, 2 and 4 require q=2; Theorem 3 allows q>=1; Theorem 5 assumes neither condition; Theorems 6-10 use (19).
Theorem 1 explicitly includes priors truncated at k=n, setting later coefficients to zero. That extra assertion is absent from Theorem 2 and is not propagated by analogy.
Theorem 3 requires alpha>=beta+1/q in the polynomial-scale branch. Theorem 5 allows any alpha>0 and has no corresponding lower bound by beta. These parameter ranges are not homogenized.

Theorem 4 prints sigma_k in its final (6) branch even though its prior is defined by the wavelet construction (4). Preserve the original symbol and record the apparent indexing inconsistency instead of silently changing it to s_l.

Sobolev (9) and Hölder (10) balls use non-strict inequalities, while Besov (11) uses a strict inequality. Coefficient definitions are primary; identifying them with classical spaces requires the source basis conditions. Equal spaces at r=2 do not make the printed strict and non-strict balls identical.

The weighted space (17) assumes w_l>=1 for l>=0, but Theorem 5 prints weights l^(1+kappa+epsilon) and l^((1+kappa+epsilon)/2), both zero at l=0. This finite-level convention is unresolved; neither the index origin nor the weights are silently repaired.

Theorem 5 compares the ordinary posterior after the data-dependent affine map tau with the law of the standard Gaussian coefficient sequence. It uses the separable vanishing-level space M0, not the whole nonseparable bounded sequence space M.

The bounded-Lipschitz metric is named but its exact test-function normalization is not supplied. The source claim about metrizing weak convergence is preserved; the theorem applies it on the separable space M0.

Theorem 6 requires alpha>1/2 in its polynomial branch and uses the general (21) scale in the other branch. Its two rate formulas differ from the two supremum-norm rates of Theorem 7. Unlike Theorem 7, its printed statement does not contain an explicit for-large-enough-n clause.

Theorem 8 refers to Theorem 7 for prior parameters and rates, not merely as a proof citation. Both branches are unpacked, including beta<=alpha in the polynomial branch. The original density-map paragraph first illustrates (4),(5), but its map itself is used with both branches by the theorem.

Theorem 9 refers to Theorem 6 for parameters and rates, whereas the preceding classification prior sentence mentions (4),(6) or (4),(5). Preserve both source passages; the theorem reference controls recorded branch parameters, with the basis discrepancy explicitly unresolved.

The classification covariate domain is [0,1]^d for d>=1, while the preceding series bases and smoothness balls are defined on [0,1]. The main-text classification paragraph does not supply a multivariate basis or dimension-dependent rate convention; no such construction is invented.

Theorem 9 prints the joint density difference p_f-p_f0 in the G,1 norm defined on X alone. The capital G is not separately defined there. Preserve this unresolved source-domain issue instead of substituting the regression difference h_f-h_f0.

The posterior power is defined for 0<rho<=1. Theorems 8-10 state rho<1 within this range, so their effective range is 0<rho<1; nonpositive powers are not included. Theorem 8 explicitly states M(rho)>0 while Theorem 9 does not print that inequality.

The normalization map for densities and logistic map for binary regression take an input function or prior. Their introductory prior examples do not impose fixed scale dependencies on every application; the theorem selects its branch explicitly.

Theorem 10 has only the wavelet scale (5), the tail bound (19), and the Besov regularity restriction. Do not add Theorem 4's polynomial branch or moment assumption merely because the discussion compares the results.

Usual L1, L2 and supremum norms, expectations, iid Gaussian distributions, coefficient inner products, measure pushforwards and asymptotic constants are ambient. The exact G,1 norm use remains unresolved as described above. Logarithmic rate multipliers are bound within the statements.

Proof-only posterior coordinate estimates, testing and sieve constructions, the displayed application to primitive functions, and simulation-specific forward operators are not required to state these ten theorems. External references and appendix proofs are not imported.

value: The registered source is the 74-page arXiv:2211.00488v1 PDF dated 1 November 2022. Main text and references end after [ZSF22] on page 28. The separately inspected Appendix A heading is on page 29; no appendix bodies were read.

Nine main-text Theorems are stored in source order: 3.1-3.3, 4.1-4.5 and 5.1. Theorem 4.1 remains included despite its citation to [LM19]. Proposition 5.1, Corollary 4.1 and numbered remarks remain outside this inventory.

Theorem 4.2 continues onto page 10 and ends with its null-estimator attainment sentence. Theorem 5.1 continues onto page 15; the threshold table inserted before its two clauses is not part of its statement.

The general model has fixed known factor-row distributions and fixed rank, independent across rows and between factors and noise. Priors depending on n,d, proportional-aspect-ratio results and swapped-factor analogies are not silently substituted for this scope.
The exact scales are n^(-1/2) in (4) and (nd)^(-1/4) in (9). Symmetric model (10) uses q_Theta/n times the Gram matrix and a GOE with diagonal variance 2/n and off-diagonal variance 1/n.

Q_Lambda and Q_Theta are uncentered second moments, not general covariance matrices. The full Remark 3.1 conditions and the explicit Theta normalization selected in Theorem 4.3 are recorded separately. The symmetric comparison model itself requires no Theta prior or Assumption 4.1.

Before equation (5), the source writes that the column-space projection matrices P and P-hat lie in O(n), although O(n) is defined as the orthogonal group. Nontrivial projections are not orthogonal matrices. Preserve this apparent source error, not a repaired definition.

The source calls alpha the principal angle, while the operator-norm formula corresponds to the largest relevant angle for equal-dimensional subspaces. Finite-sample rank degeneracy of Lambda and repeated-eigenvalue choices are not explicitly addressed. The projector formula and spectral normalization are preserved.

Claim 2 of Theorem 3.1 explicitly adds a 4+epsilon moment of Lambda_0 for Gram-matrix consistency. Claim 3 separately states an orthogonal distributional-identifiability condition. The word further leaves some scope ambiguity; extraction treats the separately numbered claims as additions to the common opening hypotheses and records, rather than invents, any cumulative moment requirement.

Theorem 3.3 cites Theorem 3.1 claim 3. It does not itself print the additional fourth moment of Theta_0 used in Theorem 3.2's matrix-risk lower bound. Do not import that fourth moment merely by comparing the two conclusions; all literal assumptions remain available for later formalization.

Theorem 4.1 prints Q-star(s) in a formula otherwise parameterized by q_Theta, without binding s. The adjacent functional suggests s=q_Theta^2, but the original statement is retained and the substitution is not silently performed.

Equation (13) is introduced for s>0, while Theorem 4.1 and threshold definition (26) also use q_Theta=0. A zero-s extension is not separately defined there. The source argmax is not asserted unique, and the countable exception in Theorem 4.1 applies only to its MMSE conclusion.

Theorem 4.2 has no zero-mean or sub-Gaussian requirement from Assumption 4.1, which is introduced later for the Lambda-estimation section. Its two bounds allow a nonzero Theta mean and require a fourth moment only for the second bound.

Assumption 4.1 requires zero first and full third tensor moments of Theta_0, but not of Lambda_0. Both priors are sub-Gaussian. The main text does not give a precise vector sub-Gaussian norm convention, and appendix definitions are not imported.

Theorems 4.4 and 4.5 refer to conditions of Theorem 4.3; they do not need its mutual-information objects merely because those objects occur in its conclusion. Likewise Theorem 4.5 does not depend on the perturbation model solely because its proof uses Theorem 4.4.

Theorem 4.4 first gives a liminf lower bound for the unperturbed risk, then a vanishing-side-channel limsup upper bound. Epsilon tends to zero after the n,d limit. The independent extra observation is available together with A, not in place of A. Generic equality without extra assumptions is not claimed.

Theorem 4.5 requires at least one of alternatives (a), (b) and (c), not all three. Bounded support and the final countable-exception qualification belong to (b). The rank-one scalar-channel condition belongs only to (c). Logarithmic powers and the two aspect-ratio inequalities are retained exactly.

Theorem 4.5(c) prints global maximum for Psi(gamma,s)=s^2/4+gamma^2/(4s)-gamma/2+I(gamma) over gamma>0. If I is the stated Gaussian-channel mutual information, it is nonnegative, so for fixed s>0 this displayed expression is unbounded above. The maximum requirement is therefore an apparent source inconsistency. Do not replace maximum with minimum, change the signs or certify this alternative as meaningful.

Theorem 5.1 uses uniform one-hot labels and iid random center rows with vanishing first/third moments and covariance q_Theta I_k. The signed two-cluster encoding and its threshold from Proposition 5.1 are different and are not imported.
