value: The inspected source is the registered 86-page arXiv:2109.13601v2 PDF dated 30 August 2023. The main paper, including its references, ends on page 33 after reference [48]. The supplementary material begins on page 34 with Section S-1.

Initial heading location encountered supplementary theorem labels; these labels were excluded. Subsequent extraction and mathematical review were confined to pages 1-33. Supplementary theorem bodies are not used as census content.

There are nine main-text Theorems. Theorem 4 continues from page 15 to page 16, including attainment by a strict-threshold rule. Theorem 8 continues from page 23 to page 24. Theorems 7 and 9 are complete on pages 22 and 24, respectively.

The source distinguishes Fraktur R (combined risk), ordinary R only in real-space notation through blackboard R, the density phi and testing rule varphi, upper-tail Phi-bar and CDF Phi, bold italic strength vector a and scalar threshold a. The procedure class S_A is calligraphic.

The sparse regime is n to infinity, s_n to infinity and n/s_n to infinity. Polynomial sparsity with unknown c<1 is extra. The general density model has independent coordinates and does not assume identically distributed coordinates or additive noise.

The false discovery proportion divides by the random rejection count truncated below by one. FNR divides by the deterministic true support count truncated below by one. Combined risk is their sum, while classification loss is an unnormalized error count.

The beta-min class (9) has exactly s_n nonzero entries, although ell0[s_n] allows fewer. Formula (9) permits a in R while its explanatory prose mentions a>0; the limiting negative-offset cases in the theorems are retained without imposing positivity of a_b.

Theorem 2 explicitly covers fixed b and b_n tending to positive infinity, but does not include negative infinity. The latter is discussed in Remark 1, not appended to this theorem. Theorems 1,3,7 do explicitly cover both infinite limits.

The main-text BH description does not provide the precise intersection/step-up convention in S-18. The empirical Bayes description gives null-probability thresholding and marginal maximum likelihood but defers the particular spike-and-slab prior, slab and optimization details to Section S-8 and S-29. These remain unresolved; no textbook replacement is inserted.

Theorem 2 imposes the polynomial sparsity and vanishing-level/log-level condition on its BH branch, while the empirical Bayes branch has a fixed posterior threshold t in (0,1). Theorem 7 again gives separate procedure alternatives, with the parenthetical polynomial sparsity attached to BH; the subsequent discussion confirms the negative-infinity case for the empirical Bayes rule without extra assumptions.

Sparsity preservation is a uniform o(1) probability of exceeding A_n s_n rejections, not a deterministic cap or expected-count bound. The source takes an infimum over classes of procedure sequences satisfying this asymptotic property; preserve that quantifier formulation rather than replacing it by a per-n admissibility condition.

The conditions on B_n in Theorems 3 and 6 use underlined lim, explicitly defined as liminf in Section 1.8. The squared B_n bound in Theorem 3 has exponent (log(n/s_n))^(1/4); in Theorem 6 it uses one third of (n/s_n) times the perturbed null tail.

Assumption 1 consists of common Lipschitz, positivity and sharp-tail conditions plus one of two alternatives. Branch A and branch B are not conjoined. Their respective risk expressions are Lambda_n and 2 Lambda_n-1, and the same branch choice is preserved in Theorems 4-6.

Branch A reflects both parameter and observation signs and imposes likelihood-ratio monotonicity for a>0 on the whole real line. Branch B is even in the observation and imposes monotonicity on the positive half-line. Branch B does not explicitly assert f_{-a}=f_a despite the subsequent absolute-signal convention; this difference is retained without adding a symmetry assumption.

The heterogeneous class (21) has strictly positive a_j and existentially matches them to distinct unknown signal locations. Lambda_n uses CDF F_{a_j}(a_n^*), not the tail, and its theta form averages over absolute nonzero signal magnitudes. Shared notation does not identify this class with the simpler beta-min class.

Theorem 5 retains the pointwise bound (25), the uniform bound, its concrete error expression and the branch-B replacement clause. Its theta-dependent level interval (24) must be interpreted consistently for a common uniform procedure. It does not explicitly require alpha_n to vanish, even though a vanishing alpha_n is needed to make the displayed additive error vanish in the bounded-away-from-one regime. This is recorded as a source-scope limitation.

In Theorem 5 the instruction to replace Lambda_n(.) by 2 Lambda_n(.)-1 under branch B is preserved verbatim. How this replacement is applied to the referenced level condition is not expanded into a rewritten theorem. The branch resolution records the effective FNR expression without making both branches simultaneous.

Theorem 6 inherits the settings and branch-dependent conclusions of Theorem 4 but changes the loss to FNR and restricts the infimum to sparsity-preserving procedure sequences. The combined-risk definition is not imported as an extra loss component merely because it is named in the replacement instruction.

The Subbotin location model has shape zeta>1 and normalized density proportional to exp(-|x|^zeta/zeta). Gaussian noise is zeta=2; Laplace zeta=1 is excluded. Its default critical threshold is not the larger optimized threshold t_n^* used in Theorem 8. The claim that Assumption 1A holds is a source assertion, not an extra model hypothesis for Theorem 8.

Theorem 7 uses the union over support sizes (31) and normalizes by the upper bound s_n. Its boundary a_b retains s_n while the union index s varies. All-zero vectors are included; this is distinct from the exact-support class used in Theorems 1-3.

The large-signal class uses fixed constants 0<a<b, beta in (0,1), r>beta and support sizes between a n^(1-beta) and b n^(1-beta). These a,b are unrelated to the earlier scalar separation and boundary offset. Nonzero amplitudes need not be equal.

Theorem 8 binds kappa as the unique root in (0,r/2^zeta), gives both equal formulas for t_n^*, and states rate equivalence with the logarithmic denominator. Its classification statement normalizes by n^(1-beta), not by the unknown exact support. The threshold uses >=, whereas Theorem 4 prints >.

Theorem 9 preserves its own limited summary form: full simultaneous adaptation is impossible, known exact sparsity permits adaptation to r, known r permits adaptation to beta, and simultaneous adaptation is possible when kappa(r,beta,2)<1-beta. The polynomial-in-n cost is asserted only for point (i). Detailed algorithms and parameter quantifiers deferred to S-9 remain unresolved.

Initial heading-location scans encountered appendix headings, but no appendix body supplies any theorem or dependency here.

All four printed main-text Theorems are retained: 3.1 on page 17, 3.2 and 3.3 on page 20, and 3.4 on page 21. Theorem 3.1 includes the whole mean/variance formula (3.4). Proof outlines and simulations do not add theorem records.

Visual and font review corrected vector Z to bold italic in Theorem 3.2 and all supporting passages. Covariate L and l and sample vector Z and z are bold italic; the covariate and data supports are calligraphic. The law operator is also calligraphic L, distinguishable by its argument.

The distribution P and rejection probability P are ordinary italic. Population integration and empirical integration are blackboard P and P_n. Expectations are blackboard E. The normal law N is ordinary italic, not calligraphic.

The printed Lp norm in Section 2.1 omits absolute values, and the prose calls f a function on R before integrating f over the joint support. Preserve these source expressions without claiming they define a valid norm for arbitrary signed f or arbitrary joint data.

I1 is potential-outcome consistency, I2 is uniform density positivity over all treatment/covariate values in the supports, and I3 is conditional-mean ignorability. Do not replace I3 by full conditional independence.
D1 requires compact treatment support, not necessarily an interval. D2 requires twice continuously differentiable theta_0 and varpi_0. D3 bounds true nuisance functions, not the outcome Y.

D4 defines tau and assumes it is strictly positive pointwise with a uniform upper bound. There is no explicit uniform positive lower variance bound. Its final formula prints P(S_tau union S_pi union S_mu)=1, although its set definitions have zero subscripts. Preserve union and subscript mismatch; an intersection would be a stronger condition.

E(A).1 prints c1^h n^(-1/5) <= liminf h_n <= limsup h_n <= c2^h n^(-1/5), leaving n outside unnormalized limits. The later prose describes an optimal estimation bandwidth order. The original condition remains unchanged and is flagged for formalization.

E(A).2 requires both nuisance estimators to approach their respective limits at little-o sqrt(h) in a uniform norm, with at least one correct limit. E(A).4 instead measures mixed uniform-in-treatment/L2-in-covariates errors about the truth and bounds their product. These are separate conditions.

The kernel class in E(A).3 satisfies (2.8) as printed. That covering bound claims all positive tau, which allows a right side less than one for large tau. No customary tau<=1 restriction is silently inserted.

The entropy integral J_m in (2.7) uses exponent m/2, envelope-normalized covering numbers and a supremum over all probability measures inside the epsilon integral. It is not restricted to finitely supported measures.

E(B)_m preserves the printed or between the two class choices, uniformly bounded reciprocal pi-hat, and a union of continuity sets for the barred nuisance limits. Its theorem-specific instantiation is m=3, with extra J4 explicitly present only in Theorem 3.4. Remark 2.3 fixes the function classes independently of n.

Theorem 3.2 omits E(B) from its assumptions. Its graph has no E(B) dependency, although it still has kernel entropy through E(A).3. Absence of an explicit nuisance entropy assumption is retained, not repaired using a proof.

The doubly robust mapping (2.2) integrates against the covariate law. The estimator (2.4) substitutes empirical covariate averages in both places and uses nuisance estimates from the same sample. No sample-splitting variant is imported from later discussion or Appendix J.

The local linear estimator minimizes a weighted empirical least-squares objective with regressor (1,(t-a)/h). K_ha has a 1/h factor, whereas the scaled convolution K_h^(s) is printed without that factor. K^(2) and K^(4) are convolution powers, not pointwise powers.

The main-text statistic is (2.5), the pseudo-outcome estimate is (2.4), and the null is (2.1). The theorem and algorithm references instead repeatedly print (J.1), (J.2) and (M.4). Main-text descriptions establish the correspondence recorded here, but the referenced appendix formulas were not inspected and no equality to a cross-fitted version is certified.

The Dudley metric uses the sum of supremum and Lipschitz seminorms, bounded by one. Theorem 3.1 approximates an n-dependent normal distribution; its b_0h includes h^(-1/2), so the statement is not converted into convergence to a fixed centered law.

Formula (3.2) retains its printed extra closing parenthesis in the subtracted squared term. It uses barred nuisance limits and their covariate averages; this differs from simply substituting the true nuisance functions. Its source-derived keyword is limit distribution, with the original preparatory formula preserved separately from theorem text.

Theorem 3.2 binds g, c_0 and delta_n inline. It requires g not identically zero, weighted mean zero with varpi printed without a zero subscript, delta_n tending to infinity, and n^(1/40)/delta_n tending to zero. The unsubscripted varpi is not otherwise defined in the admitted main text. These conditions do not assert delta_n times the local scale tends to zero.

The two bootstrap conclusions print b_h, while Theorem 3.1 defines b_0h. No separate b_h definition was found in the admitted main text. The census preserves the symbol and flags the target-mean mismatch rather than claiming it is verified notation for b_0h.

Theorem 3.3 uses Rademacher residuals centered at the estimated null mean. Theorem 3.4 centers residuals at the local fitted curve, while still centering bootstrap responses at the original mean. The replaced null-centered residual definition is not a dependency of the smoother-centered procedure.

Theorem 3.4 explicitly imposes J4 finiteness for both nuisance classes. Remark 2.2 and the pre-bootstrap proof discussion refer more broadly to fourth-order entropy; this tension does not authorize modifying the original Theorem 3.3 statement.

The bootstrap algorithms keep A_i fixed and resample signs of residuals. The source prescribes per-observation draws without separately stating their conditional independence. No nuisance refitting step is specified in these theorem-specific definitions. The auxiliary two-point distribution is an alternative method option, not an extra theorem branch.

User-specified w is required to be continuously differentiable on the treatment support in Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 and inherited by 3.3 and 3.4. Nonnegativity, strict positivity and normalization of w are not explicitly imposed and are not added.

No appendix-only theorem, proof, simulation model, real-data specification or presumed library availability contributes to this census. Unresolved source references and internal source issues do not mean the original statement has been omitted or proved false; they identify what a subsequent formalizer cannot silently assume.

The randomized sequence is y_tau=z_tau+psi_tau with iid standard normal z_tau. The introductory equal-size description uses n=N/m, whereas the two model-specific theorems allow unequal n_j of comparable order. Their sample mean and loss denominators are n_j, not a substituted common n. The distributed partition gives N=sum_j n_j.

Section 1.2 prints a_n asymp b_n as simultaneous O(b_n) and Theta(b_n). This redundant/nonstandard presentation is retained, rather than replaced by another asymptotic convention. Generic constants are independent of m,n,p as printed.
Theorem 2 uses s-bar=|S-bar| for the majority-vector support, whereas Theorems 3 and 4 use s=|supp(theta*)|. Selection count s-tilde is a third quantity. Do not replace any one of them with another.

Majority Vote requires more than half of all votes for a nonzero sign; ties and any remaining case return zero. The vote counts (1) are auxiliary definitions shared by the majority, stability and utility passages.

The stability prose describes a minimal flip count, but (4) is a signed vote-margin formula. For example three positive votes give score 3, although flipping two entries suffices to change the majority. Preserve the formula and prose separately from this issue; do not repair the definition.
The opening of Section 2.3 repeats N_l^+ twice in its list, where (1) has positive, negative and null counts. The duplicate is retained in the original passage.

The peeling score f^S has a negative minimum for the zero-majority branch. The utility f_l(.,0) in (5) has the positive minimum. Theorem 2 calls its f_l quantity a stability function, but its formula refers to (5), not f^S in (4).

Algorithm 1 selects without replacement by fresh noisy maximization. Its displayed sampling line does not explicitly say independent or specify tie breaking. An eventual implementation needs these conventions; they are not inserted into the original algorithm.

Algorithm 2 calls Peeling with epsilon/2 and delta/2, then draws signs using epsilon-prime=epsilon/(4 sqrt(2 s-tilde log(2/delta))) and a further divisor 4 in every utility exponent. These distinct factors and logarithms are preserved.

Algorithm 2 returns a support and a set of nonzero signs, while later algorithms and theorems use a full indexed sign vector. Zero extension and coordinate association are implicit; plain unordered sets alone do not encode the vector. The graph preserves the algorithm and flags this output convention.

The prose on page 11 says the algorithm always outputs a non-empty set of signs, but its printed output may be empty if all selected draws are zero. This claim is not added to the theorem statements or algorithm definition.

The algorithm formulas require positive epsilon, a suitable delta strictly between zero and one, and an integer selection count at most p. Theorem 3 contains an otherwise unused gamma_1>0 before its conclusion. The symbol is retained and its role remains unspecified within the main text.

Theorem 3 imposes only a lower bound on lambda_N in (11), and (12) does not compare the signal with the chosen lambda_N. Arbitrarily large thresholds are not ruled out by the printed hypotheses. An intended upper bound or calibrated choice is unresolved; no hidden condition is added.

The mean distribution family bounds third absolute centered moments coordinatewise. It does not impose coordinate independence, bounded observations, or an explicit positive lower bound on coordinate variances.

Theorem 4 uses equality in (18), unlike the inequality in Theorem 3(11). Its signal condition includes the random maximum over lambda_j and holds with probability tending to one, as confirmed by commentary on page 18.

The minimum over a possibly empty population support and maximum over an empty complement are not assigned conventions in the source. Sign recovery of the zero vector or full-support cases need these conventions if included.

Global sensitivity and the exponential-mechanism/composition lemmas motivate the privacy proof. The numbered algorithms give their sampling probabilities explicitly. Proof tools are not automatically theorem-statement dependencies; Definition 2 is retained as auxiliary source context.

Theorem 2 explicitly takes probability only over the mechanism given signs. Model-specific limiting probabilities combine data and mechanism randomness under the usual algorithm construction; randomness and conditional versus joint law are not conflated.

Source hypotheses about rates concern sequences as N grows; p,m,n,n_j and the selection count may vary. The source does not fully quantify dependence of epsilon and delta or uniformity in changing privacy parameters. No stronger uniform theorem is claimed.

value: The source is the registered 67-page arXiv:2309.15300v1 PDF dated 26 September 2023. Main text ends on page 29; the separate supplement beginning on page 30 and its references were not read.

All eight Theorems are preserved with their stable IDs and complete original statements. Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 include both their basic and additional-regularity branches. Main-text Lemmas, Corollaries and Remarks are not inventoried as Theorems.

The old D13 joined posterior-contraction prose with a different theorem conclusion. It is retired, with the page-5 context preserved as A3 and Theorem 5.2 retained in the inventory. Ordinary convergence-in-probability and O_P notation remain ambient, not an invented definition.

Underlying probability measures, absolutely continuous laws and Borel sets are preserved separately in A1. A moment-class dependency requires an actual use of a finite or bounded moment class; it is not inferred from merely being a probability measure.

The general Wasserstein definition is D3. The quantile/CDF formulas (2.1)–(2.2) in A2 require dimension one, and their quantile infimum uses a strict >s. They are not a general multivariate CDF formula.

The source max-sliced W_p definition ends with a maximum of W_1 even for general p. A4 preserves this index mismatch. The stated strong equivalence in (2.4) is archived as source content, not independently established or certified here.

Theorem 3.1 places its projected-density L1 norm on a continuation line after the maximized parentheses in (3.5). The intended product depends on the same direction v and is naturally included in the maximization; original placement is preserved and no normalized scope is silently substituted.

The active-coordinate set I_h^*(v), h, T and the extra bias inequality are locally bound in Theorem 3.1. Assumption 3.2 and kernel (a) concern only its additional-regularity branch, as in Theorem 4.1.

The bias definition accepts a supplied kernel. It does not itself assert condition (a); the two relevant theorem branches require that condition separately. The source kernel and its projected version may be signed, so their pushforward notation extends beyond the probability-law definition in D2.

The Fourier convention uses a positive imaginary exponent and inverse transform with negative exponent and the printed 2pi factor. Complex fractional powers need a branch convention not explicitly supplied in the main text.

Assumption 3.1 bounds reciprocal Fourier derivatives of orders zero and one and requires first moments and no Fourier zeros. Theorem 5.1 instead bounds derivatives of the Fourier transform itself through order two. These are distinct hypotheses; no proof-based edge identifies them.

Theorem 4.1 uses an observation-law moment sieve M_(4+delta)(mu_Y), not a signal-law sieve. It also requires entropy, outside-prior mass and a KL small-ball probability. The KL neighborhood bounds the raw second log-ratio moment, not its variance.

Packing is defined with separation at least epsilon, and its metric can be Hellinger or L1. Hellinger has no 1/sqrt(2) factor. The metric name d in (4.1) is overloaded with the dimension d and is resolved by context.

The posterior formula needs finite positive normalizing likelihood and measurable sets. Later Pi(mu_Y:...) denotes the induced posterior under convolution, while the prior is specified through the signal law or its mixing parameters. The source identifies observation probability laws with their densities when applying metrics and entropy.

The source names the Dirichlet process with finite positive base measure but does not construct its finite-dimensional distributions. That named prior is an external mathematical prerequisite, not an invented source definition. The product prior in A7 specifies independence of mixing law and scale.

The Gaussian shorthand phi_sigma denotes the centered location-scale density. A positive scale is implicit. Assumptions 4.1 and 4.2 impose separate base and scale-tail restrictions; their iota and varpi bounds are strengthened only in Theorems 4.3 and 4.5.

Theorems 4.2 and 4.4 assert that the conditions in (4.1) are satisfied, in addition to density posterior contraction. Their statements do not rebind every sieve constant or delta from Theorem 4.1; these are inherited conditions whose exact scope is retained.

Theorem 4.5 inherits the sampling-density assumptions and the prior of Theorem 4.4, with iota,varpi>1. It does not inherit the conclusion (4.1) as a new hypothesis, nor Assumption 3.2 merely because a proof uses the general contraction theorem.

Assumption 4.3 is a global univariate density bound with exponent 1+C0>1. Theorem 5.2 requires only an arbitrary positive multivariate exponential rate outside a compact set. Their common keyword does not make the conditions equivalent.

Assumption 4.4 controls both exponential tilts b=minus/plus one half in a Fourier Sobolev norm. It is not the unweighted Sobolev ball in Theorem 5.1, nor the projected L1 regularity in Assumption 3.2.

Assumption 4.5 preserves its envelope ratio, exponential weight and the smallest integer m at least max(2,(alpha+2)/2). The source does not state a convention for L0/f0X at zeros of f0X; this remains an interpretation issue rather than a rewritten assumption.

The cutoff tau is only partially specified in the main text; the external construction in reference [6] is not imported. Its Fourier bound is (16^2/15) exp(-sqrt(|x|/15)), with the divisor inside the square root. Do not invent a unique transition on 1<=|u|<=17/15.

The raw deconvolution integral in D23 is retained as printed without adding a real-part operation. It need not be nonnegative; the associated signed measure and projected CDF notation require the signed interpretation implicit in the source.

The approximate minimizer D24 is probability-valued and has O(n^-1/2) slack against every candidate first-moment law. Its measurable selection and existence are not constructed in the main-text definition; the raw estimator is not substituted for it.

Theorem 5.2 uses the standing iid convolution model and standard Laplace noise, so beta=2 in its preceding bandwidth. Its stated rate is n^(-1/(4d+1)); the following extension paragraph prints a different rate and assumption reference and is not used to alter the theorem.

Theorem 5.1 is a liminf lower bound with strict >C, a supremum over the intersection of a bounded first-moment probability class and a Sobolev ball, and every estimator. A fixed alpha is not a new adaptive procedure, and proof-only constructions are not extracted as dependencies.

Empirical measure P_n in the characteristic function, product sampling expectation, CDFs and density notation, Euclidean norms, Lebesgue integrals and probabilistic order are ambient standard notation. Where the source only uses these symbols, no invented verbatim definition is provided.

Constants in lesssim are described on page 7 as universal or dependent only on the true sampling law. Uniformity over directions and sieve elements is preserved where the theorem explicitly demands it; parameter-uniform results not stated in the source are not claimed.

Source statements, source identities and local dependencies have been reviewed. This census does not certify the correctness of proofs or external cited results, and no excluded supplementary assumptions are silently supplied.

The source calls the set of square-integrable measurable functions a Hilbert space but does not state the almost-everywhere quotient or underlying measure-space assumptions needed for a definite L2 norm.
The bounded function domain is printed as blackboard C. It is a domain of integration in this real function-space model, not an asserted complex scalar field.
The general Lp expression is defined for p>=1, but membership in L2 on a bounded domain alone does not ensure finite Lp norm for p>2. No such implication is inserted.
The source says operation norm when defining the continuous-operator norm; the original wording is retained.

Assumption 1(i) calls eta_it iid, while the adjacent discussion permits cross-subject correlation and varying distributions. It is interpreted temporally for each subject; Theorem 4 separately adds independence over i.
Assumption 1(ii) defines eta-tilde_Nt using eta_is on the right with no bound s. The source subscript mismatch is preserved rather than replacing s by t.

The left side of (2.6) uses an O-subscript norm on a sum of random Hilbert-space elements, although O was defined for operators. The printed expression is retained; its intended norm remains unresolved.
The coefficient condition sums j times max_i ||A_ij||_O starting at j=0. This gives no uniform bound on A_i0 by itself. No unprinted lag-zero bound is added.

Convergence mode of the infinite random-element series and coefficient-operator sum is not separately stated. The source assumes these objects exist under its standing setup; the census does not prove convergence.
Exponential integrability is stated for any i with positive bounded c_eta. A uniform numerical upper bound on these expectations and on all asymptotic constants is not explicitly supplied.
The cross-sectional moment restriction quantifies over any sequence B_i and 0<=iota<=1. Dependence of the hidden big-O constant on that sequence is not spelled out.

The covariance-kernel limit is pointwise as written. Compactness, trace summability, eigenfunction normalization and a topology for operator convergence are not explicitly established by the eigenpair passage.

Theorem 1 uses an infinite eigenvalue-weighted Brownian-bridge series and a supremum; convergence and measurability conditions are not stated separately. These are source well-definedness obligations, not extra extracted assumptions.
Theorem 1 names an upper alpha-quantile without specifying alpha in (0,1) or a generalized-inverse/tie convention. No unique critical value is invented.
Theorem 1 distinguishes joint N,T limits from its T-only PE statement. The kappa=0 growth case permits bounded N and is compatible with the latter, but not a joint N->infinity branch.
The prescribed log-log threshold may be nonpositive or undefined for small N vee T. The asymptotic setup implicitly uses sufficiently large indices; no finite-sample truncation is inserted.
The PE component uses strict >xi_NT, whereas the detected-subject set uses >=xi_NT and its complement <xi_NT. The difference at equality is preserved.
The deterministic mean process (3.9) is centered with x, while the data CUSUMs use floor(Tx)/T. Its normalization is 1/sqrt(T), without an added sqrt(N). Both printed differences are preserved.
Break locations are treated as integer sample indices in estimator maximizations, but the initial model does not explicitly state their integer or interior domain.
The individual and pooled argmax formulas do not specify tie-breaking or measurable selection. The census preserves argmax rather than choosing a minimizer/maximizer convention.

The individual estimator is defined only on the detected set, while Theorem 2 takes a maximum over the true broken set. Extension on missed-subject events is not specified; the first conclusion establishes correct detection asymptotically.
The minimum over true broken subjects and the latent partition require nonempty groups in the estimation regime. Empty-set conventions are not stated in the theorem hypotheses.
The paragraph after (4.6) equates all b_k although the structure orders them strictly. The common-break case is consistent with K0=1; the original sentence is preserved separately.
Largest-gap selection does not specify how equal gaps are ordered. Coincident selected boundaries can create empty candidate clusters; no repair is invented.
The last cluster interval ends strictly before T, while individual argmax candidates include T. Subjects estimated at T are not assigned by the printed half-open intervals.
The criterion minimizes over 1<=K<=K-bar without spelling out K<=number of detected subjects, nonempty candidate clusters, or K-bar>=K0. These are unresolved domain requirements.
The within-cluster average of integer break estimates can be noninteger, yet is used directly as a summation limit and denominator in (4.8). No floor, rounding or interpolation convention is stated.
The residual average divides by the detected-set size and takes log V(K). Empty detected sets, zero residuals and zero pre/post segment lengths have no explicit conventions.
The source says the true cluster number is determined by the formula for K-hat. The formula remains the estimator, and that wording is not silently rewritten in the original passage.
Assumption 2(i) writes exact proportional break locations and group sizes. Integer subsequences, rounding, fixed K0, and uniformity of c_k,d_k across asymptotics are implicit.
Theorem 3 states joint membership equality conditional on K-hat=K0. The conditioning event and group labels must be retained; this is not replaced with unconditional pointwise accuracy.

Theorem 4 expressly assumes only Assumption 2(i), but its estimated-group construction cites the tuning restriction in 2(iii). This is recorded as an indirect construction dependency; Assumption 2(ii) and the conclusion of Theorem 3 are not imported.

Theorem 4 asserts exact recovery using estimated groups while omitting the full hypotheses of the preceding group-consistency theorem and an explicit N=O(T^kappa) condition. The source claim is preserved without claiming its proof is valid.
The pooled estimate is indexed by estimated groups, while the conclusion ranges over true K0 groups. Its definition on events with the wrong estimated group count is not specified.
Independent standard Brownian bridges and ordinary probabilities/expectations are named source primitives. Their constructions and probability-space choices remain ambient.

Page 6 prints nu_i, without t, inside the average defining nu-tilde_t, despite defining nu_it immediately above. D8 previously inserted t; the source transcription amendment restores nu_i and leaves the source ambiguity unresolved.

value.description: Theorem 1 assumes only R<infinity, while its display divides by R squared. R=0 is not excluded explicitly. The definition also writes a maximum without establishing attainment.
The source defines a minimizer and an optimization solution without giving a tie-breaking or measurable-selection convention, or separately proving existence in the main-text definitions.
At a zero component, the printed unit-ball description permits multiple subgradients. The stationarity equation requires a compatible selection; not every unit-ball choice satisfies it.
The source calls the derivative of the nonsmooth penalized loss a Frechet derivative when a subgradient is needed at zero. The census does not turn this proof claim into a premise.

Marginal regression and empirical conditional-density kernels divide by p-hat_j without specifying behavior on zero-density events. Later high-probability bounds do not define those exceptional events.
Algorithm 1 and the estimator threshold formula divide by a residual norm. The usual zero-output convention at zero residual is implicit, not printed in these equations.
The centered initial tuple is a standing condition in the preceding algorithm discussion, not repeated in Theorem 1. The unchanged-coordinate line in Algorithm 1 omits hats.
L2 functions are treated as pointwise functions without explicitly specifying the almost-everywhere quotient or versions needed for point evaluations, derivatives and sup norms.
The normalizer integrates in x. The claimed 1<=c_h<=2 and interior equality require the later kernel conditions and sufficiently small bandwidths; they do not follow from support alone.
A tuple squared norm is a sum of component squared norms. It is distinct from the scalar squared norm of the sum in the compatibility cone and Theorem 1.

Generic integral kernels are assigned function-space operators without a separate integrability or boundedness condition. The Dirac identity representation is distributional, not an ordinary bounded kernel.

Section 3 reuses Pi-hat after subtracting the empirical marginal density from off-diagonal kernels. Its printed tilde-pi domain is [0,1] times [0,1]^d while its arguments are written as two bold vectors. Both source notation and the separate definitions are retained.

S uses population norms and S_n uses empirical norms. Their equality is conditional on density-ratio bounds. Empty S makes several gamma, bandwidth and compatibility expressions undefined unless extra conventions are supplied.

A3 bounds derivatives of active functions, but C_f,ell takes a maximum over all components. Inactive components vanish only in the population L2 sense; representative and differentiability conventions are implicit.
A2 prints an ambiguous coordinate-domain clause in its Lipschitz supremum. It is preserved rather than silently rewritten as a different quantified condition.

A6 is a conditional subexponential MGF bound over a finite transform-parameter interval. The source does not identify sigma squared as the error variance; the response second moment may diverge with dimension.

The compatibility infimum restricts to p^h-centered tuples with a nonzero active denominator. It uses expected smoothed density, not p or p-hat. Existence of an admissible tuple and empty-cone conventions are implicit.
The c_r constants are introduced by a main-text high-probability statement citing a supplementary proof. Only that explicit statement is retained; the lemma is outside scope.
The paper defines stochastic lesssim using one fixed absolute bound with probability tending to one; replacing it by generic O_P would weaken the recorded conclusion.
d, S, bandwidths and other model quantities may depend on n. Absolute constants are defined as independent of n; no extra fixed-dimensional interpretation is imposed.

The source claims that I+Pi has eigenvalues in [0,1]. This is preserved as a source assertion, not established by the census or used to infer invertibility. The source separately assumes invertibility.
Writing the inverse as I+Theta with ordinary coordinate kernels and finite row sup norms entails well-definedness conditions not separately spelled out by the main-text inverse definition.
Gamma involves the unknown true active-set size and an unspecified diverging sequence a_n. Feasibility and implementability of that theoretical tuning choice are not certified.

Theorem 6 changes the feasible set for its second branch by adding a candidate-kernel derivative constraint; it also assumes a separate derivative bound on the true kernel. These two roles are preserved separately.
A7 differentiates the discrepancy magnitude in u_j. Theorem 6 uses the second kernel coordinate x_k. These are different regularity restrictions.

The numerical approximation maximizes over i not equal to i-prime, although the continuous objective takes the supremum over the full square. The discretization is not substituted for the theorem estimator.
The q=0 formula is explicitly interpreted as a count of nonzero kernels, which entails a convention for a zero norm raised to power zero. Theorem 7 instead requires strictly positive q.

The source calls Theta_jk star the adjoint of Theta_jk but writes its kernel as Theta_kj with swapped arguments. This is the block-transpose convention as printed; the individual-block index interpretation is not silently repaired.
The source compares inverse-kernel row/column summaries with a precision-matrix sparsity parameter. The keyword is retained as an analogy; no equality of these mathematical objects is asserted.
Theorems 4 and 5 assume the conditions of Theorem 3, not its conclusion. Theorem 6 cites only A1, A2, A4, A5 and A7; Theorem 7 cites none of the A assumptions.
Theorem 4 fixes an interior point for each j, whereas Theorem 5 takes a maximum over j and a supremum over the closed unit interval. Their bandwidth restrictions are different.

The normal limit, confidence interval and test after Theorem 5 are not labeled Theorem. Their additional error independence and homoskedasticity assumptions do not become assumptions of Theorems 4 or 5.

Page 12 says the estimator vanishes for all j in S under suitable conditions, although S denotes significant components. This possible source typo is not used to alter the definition or invent a theorem.
Appendix and supplementary bodies are excluded. Main-text references to them are preserved without following the references or certifying the proofs.

value.description: The inspected arXiv v1 has a January 5, 2023 title-page date and a 4 Jan 2023 arXiv stamp. It is the registered PDF, not the published AoS text; both dates and the version-specific URL are preserved.
Theorems 2 and 4 assume weak convergence of the full sequence before identifying its limit. They do not establish existence of a limit or a convergence rate.
Iteration (3.12) uses gamma>0. Theorem 4 instead bounds eta by eta0 without explicitly identifying eta with gamma, and omits eta0>0. The original symbols and quantifiers are preserved.

Both denominators in Theorem 3 and the denominator in Theorem 6 use omega_t^(j) inside a sum indexed by l. Theorem 5 uses omega_t^(l). The printed j indices are not changed to the mathematically expected l indices.

Theorem 6 has no weight dynamics or explicit definition of omega_t^(j), although its ODE uses that symbol and its measure formula uses equal weights 1/m. The preceding equal-weight initialization is retained separately, without repairing the ODE.
The simplex allows zero weights. The j-indexed denominator in Theorem 3 is then zero for a zero-weight particle, so the displayed ODE is not defined literally on the entire stated initial simplex.

With the printed j-indexed denominators, mass preservation and agreement of Theorem 3 with PDE (3.6) require clarification. Source review records the claimed equality without proving it or changing the formula.
Uniform sampling from the indexed sample can mean uniform over indices or over distinct values when observations coincide. The source does not clarify this distinction.
The ODE claims state unique solutions on any interval [0,T] without separately specifying T>=0, solution regularity, or how the assertion is quantified over the random initial locations.
Positive finite integers N, m and d are implicit in the sample averages, simplex, and equal-weight formulas. Their domains are not repeated in every theorem.

The optimization and convergence theorems use all probability measures. The WFR flow passage uses P2. A finite-second-moment restriction must not be imported into Theorems 1, 2 or 4 merely from the flow overview.
The source defines pushforward for any mapping but does not state Borel measurability. A measurable map is needed for the usual Borel image-measure construction.

The distributional-solution definition uses spatial test functions and an ordinary derivative in time. It does not specify temporal absolute continuity, pointwise versus almost-everywhere time equality, or integrability of the fields.

The overview writes a difference quotient of measures and a limit eta->0 without specifying a topology, a one-sided positive limit, or minimizer selection. It expressly leaves existence of the limiting curve untreated.
Dynamic distance displays omit explicit endpoint restrictions and admissible regularity of curves and fields. The prose supplies the endpoints but not a complete analytic domain.

The source defines a centered probability-preserving reaction action and then states a four-times-Hellinger-squared closed form. The compatibility of these two descriptions requires separate mathematical review; neither is silently substituted for the other.

The static quadratic coupling formula is stated for all probability measures. It can have infinite value without further moment assumptions; the source does not state an extended-metric convention there.
The explicit first variation has a fixed additive constant and mean -1. A generic first variation modulo constants cannot replace it unchanged in reaction formulas containing 1+delta ell_N.

The measure update definitions allow a positive step size without an explicit condition ensuring a nonnegative density multiplier. Theorems 2 and 4 discuss small steps, with the separate gamma/eta mismatch in Theorem 4.

Algorithm 1 updates locations before weights, while (3.7) updates weights then transports the intermediate measure. Its printed denominators also use j-indexed weights. The algorithm is not substituted for the iteration in Theorem 2.

A finite atomic initialization does not have full support on R^d. The source explicitly excludes Algorithm 1 from Theorem 2 coverage; analogous finite-support issues prevent treating Theorem 4 as a guarantee for arbitrary fixed particles.
Theorem 5 uses arbitrary fixed real locations introduced in preceding prose. It does not assume their randomized initialization from Algorithm 2.
Remark 1 uses x in R where Theorem 1 uses R^d. The remark is retained as source context without changing the theorem domain or dropping its second condition.
The source uses NPMLE to mean any minimizer. No tie-breaking rule or uniqueness assumption is inserted into the conditional-limit statements.
References to appendix Theorems 7 and 8 and the unnumbered continuous-time statement after Theorem 4 are not main-text Theorem environments. Appendix bodies and proof derivations are excluded.

value.description: All statements and passages refer to the registered arXiv v4, stamped 8 Jun 2024, not an assumed published-version transcription.

The general Algorithm 1 is explicitly placed in the supplement. Only the main-text reference and Theorem 1 input/output references are preserved. Its construction and omitted local dependencies remain unresolved.
General supplement Algorithm 1, main-text Algorithm 1-dagger on page 15, and Section 4 Algorithm 1 on page 26 are distinct source references. The two latter bodies are retained in full.

Section 2 assumes A contains 0 and fully observed target data. Section 3 expressly allows an unobserved target Q. Theorem 1 still writes conditional expectations given A=0 in Delta; that notation requires clarification in the general unobserved-target case.

value.description: The source is the registered 19-page arXiv v3 stamped 9 Jul 2024. It is not assumed identical to the published AoS text.
The source permits X instead of X^2 for vector fields. L2(Omega)^2 in Theorem 3 is a vector-space subscript, whereas the squared norms in (22) and Remark 1 have an external square.
The PDE space H of divergence-free zero-mean fields differs from the Gaussian RKHS calligraphic H. V uses the gradient norm, not the full inhomogeneous H1 norm.
The main-text Sobolev definition covers integer m, while Condition 1 permits real alpha>=2. Fractional periodic Sobolev and RKHS constructions are standard external notions not expanded here.

The main text defines strong by equality of (10) in H rather than just V-prime, but refers to external books for complete solution-theory details. Theorem 1 expressly specifies C([0,T],V); no other theorem gains an extra regularity premise by importing a proof.

The Lp display does not separately state strong measurability, and the L-infinity prose says time-bounded without specifying essential versus pointwise boundedness. Ordinary Bochner and function-space conventions remain external.

Theorem 1 includes coincident initial conditions but writes logarithms and ratios involving solution discrepancies. It does not explicitly define the zero-denominator limiting conventions for (14) or (15).

Equation (15) bounds an unsquared norm ratio and (16) contains exp(c2*cP). Remark 1 instead bounds the squared ratio by lambda_J and labels that bound c_P. The displays are preserved rather than reconciled by changing exponents.
Theorem 2 writes c-prime=c-prime(c,t) without introducing c in the statement. Comparability constants and their time/index uniformity are not further expanded there.
The lower bound in (18) uses log(1/discrepancy) for all positive times and natural-number indices without separately stating positivity or nonzero-denominator conventions.
The likelihood (21) writes u_theta(X_i,t_i), whereas (19) and the forward model use u_theta(t_i,X_i). The reversal is retained in the original passage.
Condition 1 uses theta=theta-prime/N^(1/(2alpha+2)); this is not the posterior contraction rate and the RKHS is that of the base prior. Sample-size dependence is retained.
The source declares the normally empty interval (T0,T] to mean {T} when T0=T>0 and uses a Dirac temporal law. This explicit exception must not be dropped.
Theorem 3 allows T0=0, while Theorem 4 requires T0>0. Theorem 5 inherits the observation setting of the conclusions it references; no minimax lower bound is asserted at T0=0.
Theorem 3 writes T_P in its prose but T_p in both displayed suprema. The preceding prediction convention also uses T_p. Preserve source case without silently rewriting the theorem.

Equation (22) identifies expectation under the uniform probability law on [0,2pi]^2 with a Lebesgue L2 norm squared without showing a volume factor. Page 4 explicitly names Lebesgue measure dx; the original equality is preserved.
Theorem 3 evaluates the PDE at the posterior mean initial condition. Nonlinearity does not permit replacing this with the posterior mean of the solution field.
Theorem 4 uses a ball radius U and positive c(U,T) without locally quantifying U>0. The preceding Proposition 1 has its own U>0; it is not silently imported as a new theorem hypothesis.
Theorem 5 says span E_J but writes E_J={e_j:j<=J}. The intended linear-span wording and the literal set notation are both retained, rather than silently replacing the original display.
Theorem 5 only states J_N=O(log log N); this upper bound alone does not ensure growth to infinity or eventual inclusion of a fixed J0. No lower growth condition is added to the source.

Equation (20) gives complex Fourier fields only up to proportionality; adjacent prose refers to real parts. Normalization, sine/cosine selection, lattice redundancy and eigenvalue-multiplicity ordering are not fully specified there.

Theorem 5 expressly reuses the conclusions of Theorem 3 with a projected prior and different rate. This must resolve all three conclusions, including the mean and forecast, without importing proof-only theorem references as extra dependencies.

Condition 2 permits p>=1, while Theorem 3.3 explicitly assumes p>=2. Theorems 3.5 and 3.6 do not repeat p>=2 in their own statements. Preserve the standing finite-moment setting and the exact stronger restrictions actually printed; do not rewrite their hypotheses.

Condition 3 asserts symmetry and bounded first absolute moment v1. Theorem 3.7 assumes Conditions 1 and 3, not Condition 2 with p=2. Surrounding prose mentioning a second moment is not an extra printed hypothesis.

Theorem 3.7 uses c1 from Proposition 3.1, whose formula contains v_p and p. The symmetry condition supplies v1, and the main theorem does not explicitly state the parameter specialization. Preserve that scope issue rather than silently imposing a second moment.

Huber loss at tau=infinity equals half the ordinary squared loss (2.3). Source prose calls these the same squared loss. Argmin locations coincide, but the source objective tolerances remain on their own scales.

Definition 2.1 bounds differences of r-th derivatives, without adding uniform bounds on the function or lower derivatives. Its prose uses partial f in the numerator, while (2.5) uses partial^r f. Preserve both source forms.
Definition 2.2 quantifies C>0 within its class formulas. Proposition 3.4 constants depend on C. A common fixed C across the entire class is not explicitly added by this extraction.

The source assumes a selected pair (beta-star,d-star)=argmin beta/t over P. It does not separately require P to be nonempty or closed, prove attainment, or select among ties. Keep this unresolved convention distinct from the ratio itself.
The coordinate map pi:[t]->[d] in Definition 2.2 is not required to be injective. The recursive l-1 occurrence is an internal definition, not a cyclic dependency or a new condition.
The source calls L_i(x)=W_i x+b_i a linear transformation, while its displayed formula is affine. Preserve the wording and the exact bias terms.

Equation (2.10) has L hidden ReLU stages and L+1 affine maps, with scalar output. Output truncation F_n(d,L,N,M) differs from the untruncated networks asserted in Theorems 4.5 and 4.6 and does not impose bounded weights.

S_n,tau(delta) and S_HN_n,tau(delta) are distinct. The first has an objective tolerance delta squared; the latter uses a min condition involving f0,tau OR an n^-100 objective tolerance. Upper bounds are uniform over the first set; lower bounds assert existence of a bad member of the second.

The source selects f0,tau from argmin over bounded measurable Theta and calls it the global minimizer. Existence, uniqueness and versions of conditional expectations are not separately formalized; asymmetric noise can make f0,tau differ from f0.

Definition 4.1 defines a risk-rate property using iid observations with standard Gaussian error and uniform design. The definition does not separately spell out noise-design independence; it refers to the standing regression setting. Do not substitute a Holder definition or import an external proof.

Theorem 4.1 and 4.2 lower bounds use liminf_n inf_architecture sup_data-law P(exists bad approximate estimator)=1. This is not an infimum over all estimators or a claim that every approximate minimizer has large error.

The source does not separately expand zero-moment and tau=infinity limit conventions in formulas involving powers, ratios and logarithms. Preserve original v_p, v2, p and tau restrictions rather than selecting unstated limits.

Conditions 2 and 3 state bounds for every x in the cube, while Section 4 says almost surely. Versions of conditional distributions outside the design support are not specified. Preserve the respective source quantifiers.

The lower-bound nu-star and nu-dagger refer to the distinct algebraic parameters defined in Theorems 3.5 and 3.6. The lower-bound source does not redefine them; all logarithmic exponents are preserved.

Equation (4.8) lists coordinate inequalities indexed by i without explicitly writing for all i=1,...,d in the set. The source coordinate interpretation is retained without inserting quantifiers into the original passage.
Theorem 4.5 sums from i=0 but specifies only (theta_1,...,theta_r) as binary. The source does not give theta_0 in that vector. Preserve the index mismatch.

Theorem 4.5 has +2 in the first depth formula, +1 in the second width formula, and a dangling closing parenthesis in its final reduction term. The source exact-fitting branch is preserved without reconciling these expressions.
Theorem 4.6 writes y_i in its hypothesis and y_alpha in the conclusion. Do not silently change the original symbol.

Theorem 4.6 describes the second network as with depth c24*L, c25*N*log2(1/Delta2), omitting the word width. The omission is retained and its intended architectural role is identified only in the separate explanation.
Theorem 4.6 permits every Delta2>0 but uses log2(1/Delta2) as a size factor. No positivity restriction or lower bound on the logarithm is added to the original statement.

Pseudo-dimension is discussed after Theorem 3.3 and its definition is deferred to Appendix A.2. No appendix body was read; its proof-oriented role is not an extra dependency of the explicit V_n formula in the theorem.

The architecture constants c3,c4 are supplied existentially by Proposition 3.4 and then reused in (3.15). They depend on composition parameters rather than being numerical constants computed by the census.

Theorem 1.9 equation (16) prints denominator 2x rather than 2*pi*x. This is retained literally and is not silently asserted to be a normalized probability density. Theorem 1.17 calls the finite-y counterpart mu_mp,y without restating its density.

Theorem 5.3 subtracts a bare contour integral of E^chi Tr G times f without a Cauchy prefactor. The following proof writes -1/(2*pi*i). The inventory preserves the statement and records the discrepancy.
Theorems 1.11, 1.17 and 1.18 explicitly require variance greater than a fixed positive c; Theorem 5.3 does not repeat such a restriction. No extra condition is inserted.

Corollaries 1.14 and 1.15 print b1 and b2 themselves in the standardized denominator, with formulas usually suggestive of variance. Neither square root nor a squared b label is supplied by the extraction.

Equation (18) defines gamma1^0 and gamma2^0 using gamma rather than gamma^0 on their right-hand sides, despite the preceding distinction. Both the source equation and the explanatory context are preserved.
C7 ends at Im z=epsilon2, whereas C3 starts at sqrt(epsilon1^2-epsilon2^2). The written inequalities do not generally make these coincide. No repair to the contour is made.

Definition 1.4 sums all eigenvalues of H. The hat-y<1 contours exclude zero and allow functions singular there. The statements do not explicitly redefine Tr f(H) as a sum only over nonzero eigenvalues; retain this unresolved convention.

H is N by N, B is p by p and they share nonzero eigenvalues. Their zero multiplicities may differ. Do not identify all spectral statistics without accounting for f(0). The unknown-mean matrices have an additional centering rank constraint.

Definitions use inverse block covariance matrices and inverse square roots. Under the all-moment assumption samples can be discrete; high-probability invertibility does not specify a value on singular samples. No pseudoinverse or conditioning convention is invented.

Assumption 1.6 has iid columns, but does not require all matrix entries to have the same distribution. Assumption 1.19 keeps the first two bullets and replaces the third; the introductory iid-column setting remains standing context.
Theorem 1.20 inherits conclusions under Assumptions 1.19 and 1.7, not under both 1.19 and the stronger all-moment Assumption 1.6. Its graph must not reach the full D13 assumption.

Assumption 1.7 permits k depending on N and states coordinatewise limits y_t -> hat-y_t for t=1,...,k. Uniformity of this indexing when k grows is not separately spelled out. Case 1 uses k~1 rather than the literal phrase fixed k.

The page-2 definition prints Y-hat_i with entries indexed by t and the range t in [[k]]. Theorem 1.18 consistently uses i in its diagonal. Preserve the source mismatch instead of rewriting the original passage.

items.value: Twelve source issues are retained separately, including the offset boundary wording, appendix-only reach/chart/partition definitions, zero-order division and swapped pullback indices in (15), mixture integration domains, prior aliases, covariance squares, local chart inverses and coefficient/quantifier scope. value.description: The offset prose says distance less than delta; its display uses distance at most delta. Both originals remain. The census does not choose an open/closed-ball convention to repair the discrepancy.

Reach is named but its definition/properties and the construction of the normal isometries are deferred to Appendix A. Main-text chart and regularity assertions are retained; the appendix construction is not fabricated or imported.

Equation (15) quantifies 0<=<k,alpha><beta, while its first exponent is omega/<k,alpha>. At k=0 this is undefined without a convention. The source also does not specify ratios where fbar=0. These are unresolved source meanings, not reasons to delete the zero order.

Equation (15) writes fbar_(x0,delta) in ratios but fbar_(delta,x0) as weight. Definition 2.2 defines only the former. The original indices and omitted differential are preserved, with the correspondence recorded as an apparent source alias.

The mixture integrals (7)-(8) are labeled R^D while P includes orientation and sometimes scale variables. Preserve the source display; the surrounding text specifies the intended product-space mixing parameters.

Table 1 combines one weight-family column and one scale-family column. MFM adds (9); DPM does not. Both use (10). Partial scales require (11), hybrid scales (12)-(13). Dependency reach is the union of these conditional branches, not their conjunction.

The source switches pi_K/Pi_K for the count law and tilde-Pi_lambda/tilde-Pi_Lambda for the random scale law. These printed aliases remain. Independent location and orientation or inverse-Gamma scale laws are examples, not new theorem conditions.
Sigma is O_x^T Delta^2 O_x: Delta contains standard deviations, not eigenvalues. Theorem 3.4 uses Delta_(1,delta)^(-1) in its coordinate formula. No square or inverse is dropped.

Theorem 3.4 places a packing in M^tau and uses chart centers x_j, although Section 2 charts are indexed by points of M. Its partition is referred to Section D.1; the main-text proof later mentions Lemma B.4. Preserve these references and this location ambiguity without importing appendix constructions.

Theorem 3.4 specifies smooth bounded d_(j,k) depending on chi_j and M, but does not give full coefficient formulas or separately describe d_0 in its statement. Retain the existential expansion. It neither asserts that g is nonnegative nor normalizes g to be a density.

Theorem 3.4 prints existence of g before for any H>0, while the packing region includes log(1/sigma) and the asserted bound uses H. Preserve that quantifier order and do not insert hidden dependence or uniformity restrictions. Positive small scales are implicit in preceding constructions; the statement itself prints sigma,delta<=1.

The main text defines offset charts on tau/2 neighborhoods but Theorem 3.4 invokes a tau-offset packing and arbitrary x. Local inverse-chart terms require a locality/extension convention not fully supplied by its statement. The theorem and appendix reference are preserved without inventing a global inverse.

value.description: The source definition C1={x in C:|z|=1} binds x but uses z in the constraint. The accompanying description says unit complex numbers. Both the printed definition and this contextual interpretation remain separate.

The printed orthogonal loss contains (1/n)||Zhat_j-Z*_j O||_F^2 with a free j and no summation. The text calls it analogous to the summed phase loss and describes stacked matrices, but does not supply a corrected display. The original is preserved and the ambiguity remains explicit.

Theorems 1 and 2 explicitly include sigma=0 consequences, while their preambles and Theorems 3-4 contain np/sigma^2. The author also says the finite-sample result covers no additive noise. No unprinted extended-real division convention is added to the original statements.

The mapping P is displayed on all square matrices but its defining polar formula assumes full rank. Estimator (13) explicitly outputs I_d for singular blocks. That fallback is retained rather than extending the polar factor arbitrarily.

The estimator definitions specify leading eigenvectors/eigenspaces without an explicit tie-selection rule. Main-text unit-vector and orthonormal-column conventions are retained. No deterministic eigensolver or measurable tie-breaking procedure is invented.

The orthogonal-model W is written in a complex ambient matrix space despite real matrix-Gaussian blocks; the Hadamard-product definition also declares a real result for complex inputs. Preserve these source type inconsistencies without discarding imaginary parts or changing the model.

Theorem 3 writes C1,C2,C3>0. Theorem 4 writes C1,C2,C3 without >0 and assumes 2<=d<=C0. The text does not separately spell out every dependence on C0. Original scopes are retained; the bounded-d result is not advertised as uniform over growing d.

items.value: Eight scope/convention issues are recorded separately. The noisy moment mean need not lie in the stated inverse domain; Theorem 4.11 prints a nonnegative difference at different parameters; the bounded set in Lemma 4.5 is called a cone. Source statements are preserved without correction or proof certification.

value.description: The author writes Z^(0)=emptyset=G^(0) and A times emptyset=A as a formal convention. This is not literal Cartesian-product set theory; preserve the printed convention and flag it for later formalization.

Q_alpha(X) is a union over all measurable output spaces. Footnote 1 explicitly replaces scalar Fisher supremum notation by a supremum over attainable real numbers; the census retains that explanation.

Theorem 4.3 applies f^{-1}:G->Theta to the noisy mean of Z_i, but no extension or fallback outside G is given. The noisy mean need not belong to G. Preserve the theorem as printed; its domain issue is not solved by the census.

Theorem 4.11 prints 0 <= sup_Q I_theta(QP)-I_theta_n1(Qhat That P) for arbitrary theta and theta_n1. Comparing information at different parameters does not by itself justify nonnegativity. Preserve the printed bound and flag its scope; the census does not certify or correct the claim.

Lemma 4.5 calls C_alpha(k) a convex cone while imposing 0<=v_j<=1. The upper bound prevents closure under arbitrary positive scaling. Preserve the set and original wording, without dropping its upper bound.
The fixed-channel MLE definition invokes q(z|x) from Lemma D.2. Its main-text integrated density and bounds are retained; the appendix lemma is not inspected or imported.

Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 retain the event estimator in compact K in their convergence statements. They do not by themselves assert unrestricted consistency without an additional tightness or compact-parameter argument.

Theorem 4.12 explicitly assumes consistency of the second-stage MLE. The procedure allows an arbitrary value when no maximizer exists. Neither consistency nor universal attainment is inferred from the efficiency conclusion.

items.value: Exact hat-wavelet implementations and the chi-numerical regularity formula live in appendices. Only the main-text descriptions, bounds, formulas and references are retained. The census does not substitute manifold regularity for the numerical condition or claim a fully specified executable neural construction.

Fourteen source scope/convention issues remain explicit, including the d=1 zero denominator, delta=0 logarithms, network coefficient/index mismatches, scaling-wavelet name reversal, Holder/Besov endpoints and exact optimizer selections. Original statements are not corrected or certified as proofs.

value.description: The overview of Theorem 5.1 imposes both regularity conditions on both maps. The formal Theorem 5.1 imposes manifold regularity on both but density regularity only on g-star. Preserve the two labeled statements separately.

Theorem 5.8 overview asserts simultaneous gamma in [1,beta+1]; the formal theorem prints [1,tilde-beta+1]. Subsequent prose extends the claimed conclusion when beta+1>=d/2. All versions retain their original ranges without merging.

Theorems 3.1 and 5.4 minimize over delta in [0,1] while using log(delta^{-1}) and possibly nonpositive powers. No endpoint convention is supplied. Theorem 5.4 also prints beta+1=d/2 in its indicator although its other terms use tilde-beta; do not silently replace it.

Global d includes 1. With tilde-beta+1=min(beta+1,d/2), the resolution denominator 2 tilde-beta+d equals zero at d=1, and [1,tilde-beta+1] is empty. No lower dimension restriction repairing these formulas is added by the census.

The GAN, optimal discriminators and Besov approximation use exact argmin/argmax without specifying measurable selection. The covering definition uses argmin as a selected cover and does not state centers must lie in F. Preserve these conventions rather than invent a selection algorithm or altered covering definition.

Page 12 initially calls psi the scaling function and phi the wavelet, while page 13 periodization and page 14 call phi the scaling function. The Euclidean l range ends at 2^p-1, but periodic/network sums end at 2^d or 2^p. Preserve the printed roles and ranges without correcting the basis.

Formula (3.11) sums over z but prints coefficient alpha(j,l,w)_i, with its bound using z. Network sums do not explicitly supply the separate constant/coarse mode used in the source bases. Logarithmic and spatial summation endpoints have no explicit rounding convention. These details remain unresolved rather than repaired.

The hat-wavelet constructions refer to (A.4), (A.5) and (A.10) and Lemmas A.1-A.2. Preserve main-text precision, coefficient and architecture formulas, but do not claim that the appendix-only neural implementation has been extracted.

The chi-numerical regularity condition in (5.1) is defined in Appendix E.1. Main text gives only a description and a claimed implication to manifold regularity. Its exact formula and admissible chi are unresolved within the permitted main-text scope.

The Hölder display places max_i before the first derivative sum and leaves the second unparenthesized. Its definition starts at eta>0, while the pushforward display invokes H^0 test functions. The finite-q Besov norm is later used at infinity and on periodic/vector spaces without all modifications written out. Preserve these conventions explicitly.

The GAN display places the summation directly before D(X_i)-D(g(U_i)) without enclosing parentheses. The accompanying empirical-loss explanation indicates paired sample terms; the original display is retained rather than silently inserting grouping into its quotation.
Formula (4.2) prints D(g(U))-D(g-prime(u)) inside its expectation, mixing uppercase U and lowercase u. Preserve this original typo separately from its apparent intended meaning.

The generic GAN definition requires Holder-bounded classes; the instantiated classes are expressed by approximate wavelet coefficients, with no explicit Holder-ball intersection in (4.1),(4.3),(5.1). Do not invent this intersection or infer exact Holder membership solely from approximation/Besov membership.

The class construction initially states eta in (0,beta+1) and delta in (0,1), then uses eta=beta+1. Global n>=1 also permits log(n)=0 and delta=1 in displayed rates/classes. The census preserves these source endpoints and does not add an unprinted sufficiently-large-n clause.

items.value: Fourteen explicit source issues retain zero-mass and atomic split conventions, scalar/vector and reciprocal distinctions, maximal versus maximum, implicit density/log domains, the contextual N reading in T5.5, and the infinite-hull uniform-separation limitation. Statements are transcribed, not repaired or proof-certified.

value.note: Exact p-variables are pivotal because their null law is uniform. Exact e-variables merely have expectation one. Pointwise expectation nontriviality, positive log e-power and a uniform positive infimum are separate definitions; preserve each theorem clause.

T3.1 and T3.4 use JA but not AC. T4.9 is a Euclidean product-measure separation result with no JA premise. T6.1(c)–(e) and T6.2(c)–(d) explicitly dispense with JA. T6.7 assumes common domination, not JA; its pivotal strengthening is Conjecture 6.8.
AC means P_i≪Q, not Q≪P_i. It is needed to define gamma, and in T4.9 only the additional k≤2 refinement imposes AC and linear independence. Common dominating R in T6.7 is a different condition.

T4.4 and T4.7 concern a maximum dominating all feasible measures. Under N, T5.3 guarantees only a maximal limit; if a maximum exists the construction converges to it. Finite SHINE outputs need not be maximal.

Proposition 4.3 explicitly calls H_x^c the closed complement, so it overlaps H_x on the hyperplane. Do not substitute the ordinary open set complement defined in general notation. Under N the overlap has zero gamma mass.

N makes the split measure unique, while uniqueness of the half-space is separately asserted for strictly positive density. The algorithm prints a unique decomposition before T5.3’s N clause; the later atomic discussion explicitly requires a selection that the paper does not specify.

The barycenter formula divides by total mass. Splitting may produce zero-mass children, and the transition formula divides by parent mass. The main text does not specify empty-child values or transitions on null states. No arbitrary conventions have been inserted.

Equation (11) alternates x_k as a vector barycenter and as a scalar first coordinate. Equation (12) is the scalar SHINE martingale. T5.3 says measures converge almost surely; the preceding coupling supplies the a.s. random-variable interpretation. Preserve the printed wording and record the distinction.

T5.5 says same conditions as T5.3, whose conclusion has an additional N branch. The rate statement’s preceding convergent-construction context uses that branch. Preserve this contextual reading separately; do not pretend T5.5 explicitly repeats N.

T5.5 requires a finite (2+epsilon)-moment for some density coordinate j and a finite inverse-square moment for some possibly different j-prime. It does not require every coordinate or one common index to satisfy both.

The e-variable is a likelihood ratio dG/dF, whereas the SHINE coordinate corresponds to dF/dG and EP_k uses minus log. Main-text formulas do not explicitly settle all zero-density/infinite-objective conventions; AC alone is not mutual equivalence. Preserve directions and do not silently impose equivalence.

The final T6.2 clause removes finiteness and JA without stating common domination, which Remark 6.3 then supplies. The remark invokes Kraft’s uniform positive TV separation from pointwise expectation improvement and from disjoint convex hulls. Those implications are not justified for arbitrary infinite families by the printed hypotheses. Preserve the unclosed formula and flag the quantifier/topology issue rather than claiming a repaired theorem or proof certification.

T6.7 prints separately closed span and convex hull inside an additional outer closure of their sum. Only the tight-Q clause replaces this by disjointness of the individually closed sets. Total variation and tightness are named but not explicitly defined in the main text.

P^k is the finite family of pure product laws P_i^k, not all mixed products and not powers of convex mixtures. L is the null-family size; the Euclidean sample-space restriction in T4.9 is separate from L=2 in T4.7.

value.note: Equation(3.8) prints y^(e)−x^T x^(e) in R(beta;gamma,omega), rather than the beta^T x^(e) of the earlier environment risk (2.5) and empirical risk. Preserve the printed x in the original passage and record the source-backed intended interpretation separately.

General objective definitions allow unequal counts and positive weights, but all main-text Section4 theorems use equal n and uniform weights. Unequal-weight/count results are deferred to AppendixA and were not read.
Sigma^(e) and its empirical version are raw second moments. Centering is a standing convention. Condition4.3 uses pooled Sigma^-1/2, not environment-specific whitening.

The objective gates its moment penalty on beta_j≠0; it is generally nonconvex. T4.2’s lower bound relative to beta* is not a global pairwise convexity claim despite the theorem title. Empirical squared means also differ from means of squared products.

Theorems apply to global minimizers. Gumbel approximations and tuning guidance are deferred to appendices, and Section6.2 states exponential computational complexity for the current global search. No guarantee for generic stationary points is inferred.

Section4.2 explicitly treats G nonempty. The supremum defining gamma*, the minimum defining s_-, beta_min and s_+, and log(|E||S*|) require nonempty families/supports or conventions not given in the main text. Keep these domains explicit without inventing values for empty minima.

G is defined by a sum of residual correlations across environments, which may cancel. It is not the union of individually endogenous variables. Condition4.5 quantifies over all S meeting G, with the differentiating environment pair allowed to depend on S.

T4.3 only yields S*⊆supp(beta-hat_Q)⊆G^c and can retain irrelevant exogenous variables. T4.5 yields equality for the l0-penalized estimator. Refitting after selection is separately described and is not the estimator in the theorem.

T4.4 first gives a p-dimensional bound with probability 1−7e^-t. Only its moreover branch imports the extra T4.3 sample bounds and gives the |G^c| bound with probability 1−14e^-t. Neither branch is silently discarded or made an unconditional conjunction.

T4.4 names c1–c4 although c4 does not appear in its formulas. T4.5 prints both s^star and s^* for the same sparsity count in epsilon(n). Preserve these source forms and do not invent another parameter or missing c4 term.

Condition4.6 gives two sample bounds, while T4.5 additionally requires a nonempty lambda interval with a two-term epsilon(n). Preserve all terms and the upper bound c2 kappa_L beta_min²; simplified asymptotic lambda ranges following the theorem are not substitutes.

The model has common conditional expectation only on S*, allowing residual dependence on other covariates. The focused linear conditions imply LLS-invariance rather than CE-invariance in general. No SCM, full exogeneity, conditional sub-Gaussian tail or residual independence is added.

value.note: The Gaussian processes coexist with an equal-joint-law copy on a possibly enriched probability space. The original variable notation suppresses this convention. The theorem rates are o_P, not the introductory classical almost-sure KMT rate.

Clipping at n^(1/p) defines X^oplus; S^oplus additionally subtracts the clipped means. T2.2’s second branch matches Cov(X^oplus) yet compares to original S. T2.4’s faster Brownian time is the second moment of the centered clipped sum, while its slower branch uses the original sum.

Condition2.3 diverges over blocks with m_n+1 terms; Condition2.4 bounds length-l second moments below by c l. A0 and A0-prime are different formulas. T2.4 and T3.2 require neither nonsingularity condition; T3.1 only uses A>1. No implication is turned into an additional dependency.

The paper calls Condition2.2 weaker than classical uniform integrability. As printed for a fixed sequence with sup over all i, taking a=1 and reparameterizing the truncation threshold yields the same criterion. Any triangular-array interpretation would need explicit index conventions absent here.
